# The Store Is the Design

**Stance: subtractive-minimal.** The question asks for four features — identity, self-description, durability, undo. This design supplies one property and derives all four:

> **The print barrier.** `c4` writes a C4 ID to stdout only after every byte that ID transitively names is durable in the store. Conversely, anything the store has ever printed can be recovered from the store alone.

Everything else is the removal of things: no new object kinds, no refs, no journal, no backup format, no snapshot registry, zero new flags, and a net *reduction* of about seven flags. One new verb (`restore`) because the existing verb set genuinely has no tree-materializer.

## The found unification (why nothing new is needed)

Two frozen facts collide productively:

1. A c4m's own ID is the ID of its canonicalized text.
2. A directory's C4 ID is the ID of the one-level canonical listing of its direct children.

In the shipped code (`c4m.Manifest.WriteCanonical`), canonicalization of a nested c4m renders **only the top-level entries** — nested children participate via their parent directory's ID field, not their own lines. Therefore *the canonical ID of a directory's description equals the directory's own ID*. A "snapshot object" does not need to be invented: it is the root's one-level listing, an ordinary plain-text store object, and its ID is simultaneously the description's identity and the root directory's identity. The store already held per-subdirectory listings (`c4 cat -r` walks them); the only gap producing founding complaint #1 was that the **root** listing was never stored and its ID never printed. The fix is two behaviors, not one feature: store the root listing too; print its ID.

This satisfies principle 1 (the best feature "turns out to already be possible") and principle 5 (nothing decorates the format; the snapshot is content referencing content).

## 1. Identity: one mechanism, two named views

There is exactly one identity mechanism: the C4 ID of some bytes; for a directory, the bytes are its one-level canonical listing, recursively (frozen Merkle rule, untouched). What varies is *which fields the description records* — and the spec already makes unrecorded fields first-class nulls (principle 11). So identity is not a new axis; it is the existing knowledge-level axis, with two levels named to users:

- **content ID** — the ID of a description that records only what the bytes determine: names, sizes, file IDs, and directory IDs computed from those (mode and timestamp null). Two trees have equal content IDs iff their contents are byte-identical — on any machine, clock, or umask. Printed by `c4 id -q`.
- **snapshot ID** — the ID of a description that records everything observed at a moment: modes, times, sizes, names, IDs. Printed by `c4 id -s` after everything it names is durable; it is the recovery handle.

A single file has one ID — its bytes — the degenerate case, unchanged (`echo x | c4`, `c4 id -q file`).

Rationale for the field split: size is a function of the bytes, so it stays in the content view (and keeps listings informative); mode is excluded because umask varies (T3 names umask explicitly); timestamp is excluded because clocks vary. Both views are legal canonical listings under the frozen grammar — nulls render `-`. Two machines' *snapshot* IDs of identical checkouts legitimately differ (they observed different mtimes); their *content* IDs are string-equal. That is the honest answer to "same content?": the tool never asserts sameness it did not compute (principle 7), and the content ID is falsifiable anywhere by recomputation (principle 10).

Three default changes make this coherent, all inside existing flags:

- `c4 id` **defaults to content mode** (`-m c`, one new value on the existing `-m s/m/f` flag). Asking "what is this?" should give the machine-independent answer; today's mtime-polluted default is precisely the founding T3 defect. Observation remains one flag away (`-m f`).
- `c4 id -s` **defaults to full mode** — preserving should record everything it can see. Ask = content, preserve = full: one sentence, applied everywhere (diff scans directories at content level too, or at the other side's knowledge level when one side is a description — the existing guided-scan behavior).
- `-q` now means "print only the ID" (was: print nothing). `-s` prints only the snapshot ID (was: the whole manifest — which is exactly the artifact complaint #1 shows users losing). Want the text? `c4 cat -r <id>`; it is in the store, which is the point.

These are breaking changes to defaults, declared openly; the crucible exists to fix defaults before freezing them. Grammar, IDs, and the Merkle rule change zero.

A uniform resolution rule (not a concept, an argument convention): wherever a verb accepts a c4m file path, it accepts a description ID, resolved from the store — `cat`, `diff`, `restore`, `id`. So `c4 id -q <snapshotID>` computes the content ID of a stored snapshot without materializing anything (projection: null the stat fields, recompute bottom-up), and `c4 diff <id> <id>` reconstructs any changeset after the fact.

## 2. Self-description: the store alone is enough

A snapshot deposits exactly two kinds of ordinary objects — file blobs, and one one-level listing text per directory *including the root* — and prints one line: the root listing's ID. There is no third artifact. Consequences:

- **T1 by construction.** Delete the tree and every file the command produced outside the store; `c4 restore <snapshotID> dir` rebuilds it, because `cat <id>` returns the root listing, whose lines carry each child's metadata and ID, recursively. The description recovers *itself* the same way content does; complaint #1 dissolves rather than being patched.
- **The receipt is falsifiable in one command**: `c4 cat -r <id> | c4 -x` reprints the same ID (the flatten rule guarantees it). A stale or corrupt store cannot bluff (principle 7).
- **Description history dedups by Merkle sharing.** Unchanged subtrees reuse the same listing objects across snapshots, so repeated snapshots cost O(changes) in both content and description — a history mechanism with no history feature.
- **Plain text all the way down** (principle 2). Store objects are files named by their IDs containing either user bytes or human-readable listing lines. With the binary lost, a shell can still recover everything: find the file named by the ID, read the listing, follow the last field. The meaning of the store outlives the tool.
- Ingesting a description (`c4 id -s file.c4m`, or a c4m on stdin) stores its full listing chain, one object per directory, so a patched description becomes restorable by pipe: `c4 patch chain.c4m | c4 id -s -`.
- The **empty description** — zero entries, zero bytes — has the fixed ID `c459dsjf…sFT` (ID of the empty string; `canonicalDirID` already hashes empty directories this way). It is defined as always resolvable. It is the pre-image of an absent target and the way to say "make this directory empty."

Naming, refs, and "which snapshot is latest" are deliberately *outside*: an ID in shell history, a text file of IDs, a git-committed lockfile line (principles 5, 6 — beside git, not instead; a lockfile is an entry). The store stays a bag of self-verifying closures; GC policy stays a non-goal, noting only that undo handles are ordinary roots you keep by keeping their IDs.

## 3. Durability: printed means durable

Protocol (semantics, stated to users; implementation follows the measured physics):

- Objects land as temp files, `fsync(2)`, atomic rename; before any ID reaches stdout, **one** full-flush barrier (`F_FULLFSYNC` on the store device) runs. Then the ID prints, then exit 0.
- Physics: per-file full-flush costs ~6.4 ms (20k files ≈ 3 minutes) and buys nothing the single end barrier doesn't; plain fsync is ~126 µs/file and the barrier ~5.4 ms. So snapshotting 20,000 files costs read+hash (disk speed, parallel) plus ≈2.5 s of sync and one 5 ms barrier — **seconds, not minutes** (T4). Same-volume APFS ingestion can clonefile (14k files ≈ 0.26 s), making store writes nearly free.
- **If the ID printed** (even if power fails one microsecond after): the snapshot and everything it names survive.
- **If it didn't print**: the run didn't happen. The source tree was never touched (snapshot is read-only on the tree); the store is unharmed — objects are self-verifying by name, so a torn object is detectably invalid and treated as absent; rerun is idempotent and cheap (dedup skips everything already present). Concurrent runs are safe for the same reason (put-by-ID, atomic rename).

Materialization mirrors ingestion: restored files are written temp+fsync+rename with one barrier before the final printed line, so the *restored tree* is also crash-durable the moment its ID appears. There is no `--no-fsync` anywhere: at 126 µs/file, durability is not worth a mode, and modes multiply states (principle 8's "fast by flag" is satisfied by having made safe fast).

## 4. Destructive-reconcile safety: undo is the same verb reading its own output

`restore` is the **only** verb that writes user trees (principle 12: one implementation per idea — the `reconcile` engine gets exactly one CLI face). `patch` returns to pure text algebra: chains in, resolved text out; pointing it at a directory errors with the correct command. That deletes the accident vector of complaint #2 *and* seven flags (`patch -s -r -q --dry-run --source --no-store --no-fsync -m` all existed to manage in-place mutation and its hand-built backup story).

`c4 restore <target> <dir>` behavior:

1. Resolve the target description (ID or c4m file). Pre-check closure: every ID it names must be resolvable; otherwise list the missing IDs on stderr and exit 1 **before touching anything** (the existing planner already refuses on missing content).
2. Snapshot `<dir>` as it stands — full mode, full print-barrier durability — and print its snapshot ID as **line 1, before the first mutation**. This is principle 8 verbatim: the backup is durable before destruction begins, and it is not a flag, it is the meaning of the verb. Cost is near-free in the common case: the pre-image scan is the same scan reconciliation needs anyway, and dedup stores only bytes the store lacks.
3. Reconcile: create/move/update/remove; apply recorded modes, times, symlinks, hard links, sequences; null fields apply platform defaults and never overwrite an existing equal file (a null is no-claim).
4. Verify by recomputation at the target's own knowledge level — a full snapshot must reproduce its snapshot ID from disk; a content-mode target must reproduce its content ID. Only then, barrier, and print the verified target ID as **line 2**.

The two-line stdout is the whole story: line 1 is where you were, line 2 is where you are, both now in the store. **Undo is `c4 restore <line 1> <dir>`** — which prints the mistake's ID as *its* line 1, so redo is also free. No trash directory, no reflog, no new state. T2 is two invocations of one verb. A no-op restore prints the same ID twice. The pre-image of an absent directory is the empty ID; restoring the empty ID empties the directory — no special cases.

`restore` has zero flags. Preview is not a mode but a verb that already exists: `c4 diff <dir> <target>` (composition over configuration); its help says so. There is deliberately no `--no-preimage`: an invertible operation needs no confirmation ceremony, and the only truly destructive verb in the suite remains `gc --force`, which already follows dry-run-by-default.

## Surface accounting and the tasks

**Concepts: 2** (content ID, snapshot ID — one sentence each, one mechanism beneath). **New verbs: 1** (`restore`). **New flags: 0** (one new *value* `c` on the existing `-m`; `-q`/`-s` outputs redefined; ~7 flags deleted from `patch`). **Grammar changes: 0. Dependencies: 0.** stdout remains byte-pure: bare IDs or c4m text, narration on stderr, explanation in `c4 explain`.

- **T1**: `c4 id -s proj/` → one ID; `rm -rf proj/`; `c4 restore <id> proj/` → byte-exact, metadata included, verified before the ID echoes.
- **T2**: wrong-directory restore prints the victim's snapshot ID first; `c4 restore <line1> dir` returns it byte-exact.
- **T3**: `c4 id -q dir` on both machines; string-equal iff contents byte-identical.
- **T4**: ~20k files in seconds (hash-bound + ≈2.5 s sync + 5 ms barrier); printed ⇒ durable; unprinted ⇒ untouched tree, consistent store, idempotent rerun.
- **T5**: `c4 cat <id>` lists (one level; `-r` for the tree); grep the name, `c4 cat <fileID> > name` extracts.

What was removed from the problem: the snapshot artifact (now ordinary content), the backup feature (now the verb's first line), the durability mode (now the meaning of printing), the second identity system (now a null-projection of the first), and a directory-mutating `patch` (now an error message that teaches `restore`).
key_decisions: The print barrier is the store's one contract: no ID reaches stdout before everything it transitively names is durable (one device flush, ~5.4ms), and any printed ID is recoverable from the store alone — identity, self-description, durability, and undo are all corollaries.

Zero new object kinds: by the existing flatten-on-canonicalize rule a description's canonical ID equals the described root's directory ID, so the 'snapshot object' is just the root's one-level listing stored like any other content; the whole fix for complaint #1 is 'store the root listing too, print its ID'.

Two named identities, one mechanism: content ID (stat-free — mode/timestamp null, size/names/IDs real; machine-, clock-, umask-independent) and snapshot ID (full observation; the recovery handle); they differ only in which fields are null, and files keep their single blob ID.

c4 id defaults flip to ask-vs-preserve: plain id scans in new content mode (-m gains value 'c'; answers T3), id -s scans full and prints only the snapshot ID (was: the whole manifest), -q now prints only the ID (was: silence) — breaking default changes accepted, grammar and Merkle rule untouched.

restore is the sole tree-writing verb and has zero flags: it always snapshots the target directory (full mode, durable, printed as line 1) before the first mutation, reconciles, verifies by recomputation at the target's own knowledge level, then prints the target ID as line 2; undo = restore line 1, redo = restore line 2.

patch is demoted to pure text algebra (chains in, resolved c4m out) and loses ~7 flags (-s, -r, -q, --dry-run, --source, --no-store, --no-fsync, -m); pointing patch at a directory errors with the restore command — the accident vector of complaint #2 is deleted, not guarded.

Durability physics: per-file F_FULLFSYNC (6.4ms → 3min/20k) is rejected; plain fsync+rename per object (~126µs) plus one end barrier gives 'printed ⇒ durable' at ~2.5s overhead per 20k files, so there is no --no-fsync mode anywhere; torn objects are self-detecting because objects verify against their names.

Uniform argument resolution: anywhere a verb takes a c4m file it also takes a description ID resolved from the store (cat, diff, id, restore), so tree-ID-from-snapshot, after-the-fact changesets (diff id id), and store-only reading need no new surface.

Nulls are the identity engine, not an edge case: a null field is 'no claim' — content IDs are the null-projection of snapshots, verification recomputes only claimed fields, and restore never rewrites a file a partial description doesn't contradict.
The empty description (zero bytes) has a fixed, always-resolvable ID: it is the pre-image of an absent directory and the way to empty one — no special cases in the undo story.

Naming/refs/GC policy stay outside the store (a kept ID is a line of text — shell history, a lockfile entry, a git-committed file); the store remains a bag of self-verifying closures beside git, not a VCS.
result.stance: Subtractive-minimal — the store is the design: one property (an ID is printed only after everything it names is durable in the store, and any printed ID is recoverable from the store alone) carries identity, self-description, durability, and undo; the surface change is +1 verb, +0 flags, −7 flags, 2 named identity concepts, 0 format changes.

C4-ID(1)

NAME
    c4 id - describe and identify files, directories, and descriptions

SYNOPSIS
    c4 id [-q] [-s] [-m MODE] [-e] [-S] [--exclude GLOB]...
          [--exclude-file FILE] [-c GUIDE] <path|c4id>...

DESCRIPTION
    Writes a plain-text description (c4m) of the given tree to stdout.
    Arguments may be directories, files, c4m files, or C4 IDs of stored
    descriptions (resolved from the store). With -q, prints only the ID
    of the description. With -s, ingests everything into the store and
    prints only the snapshot ID.

MODES (-m)
    s  structure   names only
    c  content     names, sizes, and IDs computed from bytes alone;
                   mode and timestamp are null (-). Default.
    m  metadata    names, modes, times, sizes; no IDs
    f  full        everything observed. Default when -s is given.

    -s requires a mode that records IDs (c or f).

FLAGS
    -q, --quiet          Print only the C4 ID: a file's ID, or the ID of
                         the directory description the scan produces
    -s, --store          Ingest into the store: every file's bytes and
                         every directory's one-level listing, including
                         the root. Prints the snapshot ID as the only
                         output, after everything is durable
    -m, --mode MODE      Scan mode: s, c, m, f (see MODES)
    -e, --ergonomic      Output ergonomic (aligned) form
    -S, --sequence       Detect and fold file sequences
    --exclude GLOB       Exclude pattern (repeatable)
    --exclude-file FILE  File of exclude patterns, one per line
    -c, --continue C4M   Continue from an existing c4m (used as a guide)

OUTPUT
    Without -q or -s: a c4m stream.  With -q or -s: one line, one 90-char
    C4 ID.  All narration and progress goes to stderr.

DURABILITY
    If the ID printed, the description and every byte it names survive
    power loss. If it did not print, the scanned tree was never modified,
    the store is unharmed, and re-running continues where it left off
    (objects already present are skipped). Snapshotting ~20,000 files
    takes seconds on a modern SSD; durability adds roughly 2.5s plus one
    5ms device flush, applied once before the ID prints.

EXAMPLES
    c4 id -q src/                     # content ID: same on every machine
    c4 id -q v2.c4m                   # content ID of a saved description
    c4 id -s project/                 # snapshot; prints snapshot ID
    c4 id -s -m c project/            # machine-independent snapshot
    c4 id project/ > project.c4m      # description as a file; no store
    c4 patch chain.c4m | c4 id -s -   # store a resolved description
    c4 cat -r ID | c4 -x              # recompute ID: verifies a snapshot

SEE ALSO
    c4 restore (materialize), c4 cat (read), c4 diff (compare),
    c4 gc (collect), c4 explain id (narrated walkthrough)

C4-RESTORE(1)

NAME
    c4 restore - make a directory match a description, undo-safely

SYNOPSIS
    c4 restore <target> <dir>

    target:  a description's C4 ID (snapshot ID, content ID of a stored
             description, or any stored directory listing ID), or a c4m
             file path
    dir:     the directory to reconcile; created if absent

DESCRIPTION
    Makes <dir> match <target> exactly: files are created, moved,
    updated, and removed as needed. Recorded modes, times, symlinks,
    hard links, and sequences are applied; null fields apply platform
    defaults, and files whose content already matches are left alone.

    Before anything in <dir> is modified, its current state is
    snapshotted into the store — content and description, durable —
    and that snapshot ID is printed as the first line of output. The
    prior state is always recoverable:

        c4 restore <first-line> <dir>       # undo
        c4 restore <second-line> <dir>      # redo

    Content comes from the store and from <dir> itself (moves are
    detected). If any content the target names is unavailable, restore
    lists the missing IDs on stderr and exits 1 without touching <dir>.

    restore takes no flags. To preview, diff first:

        c4 diff <dir> <target>

OUTPUT
    Exactly two lines on stdout:
      line 1: snapshot ID of <dir> as it was, printed before any change
      line 2: the target's ID, recomputed from the resulting tree and
              printed only after verification succeeds
    A no-op restore prints the same ID twice. If <dir> was absent or
    empty, line 1 is the empty description
    c459dsjfscH38cYeXXYogktxf4Cd9ibshE3BHUo6a58hBXmRQdZrAkZzsWcbWtDg5oQstpDuni4Hirj75GEmTc1sFT
    (the ID of zero bytes); restoring that ID empties the directory.

DURABILITY
    Line 1 is printed only after the prior state is fully durable, and
    always before the first modification. Line 2 is printed only after
    the restored tree is verified and durable. If power fails between
    the two lines, <dir> may hold a mix of old and new files, but both
    end states are safe in the store: re-run the same command to finish,
    or restore line 1 to go back.

EXAMPLES
    c4 restore c461iQnu...igYz proj/      # materialize a snapshot
    c4 restore $(c4 id -s good/) bad/     # copy good over bad, undoably
    c4 restore c459dsjf...c1sFT tmp/      # empty a directory, undoably

SEE ALSO
    c4 id -s (create snapshots), c4 diff (preview), c4 cat (inspect),
    c4 explain restore (narrated walkthrough)

C4-PATCH(1)  (narrowed)

SYNOPSIS
    c4 patch [-n N] [-e] <chain.c4m> [<dest.c4m>]
    c4 patch [-n N] [-e] <file.c4m>...

DESCRIPTION
    Resolve patch chains: read c4m streams, apply their patch sections,
    write the resolved description to stdout or <dest.c4m>. patch reads
    and writes c4m text only. It does not modify directories; given a
    directory argument it exits 1 with:
        patch composes descriptions; to change a directory:
        c4 restore <target> <dir>

FLAGS
    -n, --number N    Resolve to patch N (1-based; 0 = final state)
    -e, --ergonomic   Output ergonomic form

NOTE ON cat AND diff
    c4 cat <id> prints a stored object: file bytes verbatim, or a
    description (one level; -r expands the tree from the store).
    c4 diff accepts directories, c4m files, or description IDs on either
    side; directories are scanned at content level, or at the other
    side's knowledge level when one side is a description.

# Snapshot–Store–Restore as One Surface — Composition-First Candidate

## 0. Method

Stance: every capability must fall out of the existing eleven verbs and the frozen c4m grammar. I audited each of the four design areas against the existing primitives before allowing any new semantics. The result: **zero new verbs, zero new flags, two named identity concepts**. Everything else is a change of *default* in existing verbs, plus one store-resident file that is an ordinary c4m patch chain — a structure every existing chain verb (`log`, `patch -n`, `split`) already reads.

The audit found the pieces already 90% present: `c4 id -s` already stores every *directory's* one-level listing as an object; `c4 patch` already emits changesets bounded by bare IDs; `patch -n`/`split`/`log` already navigate chains; the store already writes objects durably (temp + fsync + atomic rename). What is missing is coherence: which listing gets hashed (identity), whether the description itself is captured (self-description), when the store is allowed to "speak" (durability), and whether preservation is a flag or a default (safety).

## 1. IDENTITY — two names, one mechanism

**Concept 1 — content ID.** *The ID of the bytes themselves: two files or trees have equal content IDs exactly when their contents are byte-identical — independent of machine, clock, timestamps, or permission bits.* For a file it is the C4 ID of its byte stream (unchanged, SMPTE ST 2114). For a directory it is the C4 ID of the one-level canonical listing of its direct children rendered in **content form**: mode `-`, timestamp `-`, sizes and names as-is, symlink targets as-is, each child directory represented by *its* content ID. The Merkle rule of the spec ("directory ID = ID of the one-level canonical listing of direct children") is untouched; the design pins *which* canonical listing is hashed, using the null fields the grammar already makes first-class. Nothing about the grammar changes: content form is a valid c4m stream today.

This repairs the standing determinism violation: today directory IDs hash child mtimes and modes, so identical checkouts on two machines get different IDs — an ID that does not reproduce across machines fails the project's own determinism principle and makes T3 impossible. The stats are not lost — they move to where they belong, the recorded description (mode and timestamp *columns* of the snapshot's entry lines). Identity is bytes; metadata is record.

The manifest's own computed ID (`ComputeC4ID`, the bare boundary IDs in diffs and chains, checkpoint verification) follows the same rule: **the ID a c4m denotes is its root content ID** — the ID the tree would carry as a child entry in a parent listing. This makes the spec's own composition law hold exactly: `c4 id DIR | c4 id` prints `DIR`'s ID. Diff/patch boundary IDs therefore become machine-portable, and an mtime-only change produces a patch whose entries record the metadata change while its boundary IDs are equal — valid under frozen chain semantics (only *empty* sections are rejected).

**Concept 2 — snapshot ID.** *The ID of a recorded description: the content ID of the c4m file itself, as bytes; `c4 cat` of it returns the exact description, metadata and all.* A snapshot is not a new kind of object — it is a c4m file stored as content, keyed like every other object by the hash of its bytes (its deterministic canonical encoding: sorted, canonical fields, nested with indentation — byte-identical on every machine given the same recorded fields). So there is one identity mechanism (hash of bytes / hash of canonical listing) wearing two named roles. Users see exactly two nouns: *content ID* (compare, reference, verify trees) and *snapshot ID* (retrieve a recorded description).

One acknowledged asymmetry: piping a c4m into `c4 id` yields the *denoted* tree ID, not the description-file's own ID. The snapshot ID is instead minted at ingest, recorded in the store log, and verified by the store itself: `c4 cat` checks on read that an object's bytes hash to its ID and refuses to emit otherwise. That yields a uniform, one-command falsifiability story for *every* object class — file blobs, directory listings (whose bytes are the canonical listing text, so hash-of-bytes and listing-ID coincide), and snapshot blobs.

## 2. SELF-DESCRIPTION — the store alone recovers everything

New default of the existing snapshot-with-storage paths (`c4 id -s`, bare `c4 <dir>`, and `c4 patch <dir> <dest.c4m>`): storing a tree stores **three layers plus one record**:

1. every file's bytes (existing);
2. every directory's one-level content-form listing — the Merkle graph, so `c4 cat -r <content-id>` reconstructs structure from the store (existing mechanism, now content-form, now including the root);
3. **the full snapshot c4m itself** — the exact description printed on stdout, with metadata columns — stored at its snapshot ID (this is founding complaint 1's fix: the description is content too);
4. **one entry appended to the store log**, `<store>/log.c4m`: an ordinary plain-text c4m patch chain living beside the `c4/` object trie. Each event appends one section containing one file entry — `- <event-time-UTC> <blob-size> <rootname>.c4m <snapshot-id>` — between bare checkpoint IDs. Honest c4m semantics throughout: the log *is* a catalog of c4m files, named for the trees they describe.

Because the log is an ordinary chain, the entire history surface is existing verbs: `c4 log` lists the timeline; `c4 patch` resolves the current catalog (latest snapshot per name, since a same-name entry with different fields is a modification under frozen patch semantics); `c4 patch -n N` time-travels the catalog; `c4 split` archives old history. The only additions are *default arguments*: with no c4m named, `log`, `patch`, and `gc` operate on the store log. One sentence teaches all three: *when no c4m is named, the store's log is the c4m.*

Recovery therefore needs zero retained bytes outside the store: catalog → snapshot ID → `c4 cat` → description → `c4 patch` materializes. The snapshot cannot contain its own ID (a hash cannot embed itself); the log is the external structure that names it — capabilities from the outside, referencing immutable IDs.

The log records *descriptions* (directory snapshots, ingested c4m files), never raw blob puts — `echo x | c4` does not spam the log.

`gc` keeps its mark-and-sweep and dry-run default; its default roots become every snapshot ID in any log section, so history is never silently collectible. Forgetting is explicit composition: `split` the log, move the recent half into place, `gc --force`.

## 3. DURABILITY — the store speaks only after a barrier

Grounded in the measured physics: per-file F_FULLFSYNC (~6.4 ms) is banned — 20k files would take ~3 minutes. The protocol:

**Ingest (`id -s`, bare `c4`, pre-images):** each object is written to a temp file, `fsync(2)`'d (~126 µs), and atomically renamed (existing DurableWriter). After all objects: append the log section, fsync it, then issue **one** full-device flush (F_FULLFSYNC on the log fd, ~5.4 ms) — *then* print the `recorded:` line on stderr and exit 0. Durability overhead for 20,000 files ≈ 20k × ~130 µs + 5.4 ms ≈ **2.5 s** on top of hashing I/O.

User-visible contract: **if the command reported the snapshot (or exited 0), power loss loses nothing — the snapshot, all content it references, and its log entry survive. If power fails earlier, the log is unchanged and the snapshot does not exist**; at worst the store holds orphaned-but-valid objects (harmless by content addressing; `gc` sweeps them). `c4 id` never writes to the source tree, so the tree is untouched in every case.

**Log append atomicity:** a section either appears completely or not at all. A torn tail from a crash mid-append is ignored by readers and truncated by the next append (WAL tail rule). This is reader tolerance on one file, not a grammar change — an unclosed final section is already legal in the frozen chain format; the log narrows that to "a *malformed* final section is dropped."

**Materialization (`patch → dir`):** files are written temp + fsync + atomic rename (no torn files ever visible), one final barrier before exit 0. Contract: on exit 0 the destination tree is durable. Mid-command power loss leaves a mix of old and new *whole* files, recoverable in either direction (pre-image via the log, or re-run the patch — reconcile is idempotent toward its target). `--no-fsync` (existing flag) keeps atomic visibility but waives the power-loss claim for destination files — safe to offer because everything remains re-materializable from the store, which the same run has already made durable.

## 4. DESTRUCTIVE-RECONCILE SAFETY — preserved by default, undoable by construction

Founding complaint 2's fix is one default: **every reconcile records a durable pre-image before its first destructive operation.** `c4 patch <target> <dir>` now (a) guided-scans the destination, (b) ingests its content and stores its snapshot, (c) appends the log entry, (d) issues the barrier, and only then (e) mutates. Dedup makes (b) nearly free when the content is already known; when it isn't — the wrong-directory accident — the ingest is exactly the work that makes the accident survivable. If the destination is absent or empty there is nothing to preserve and nothing is recorded; a no-op reconcile records nothing.

The undo story is not a feature; it is the log: the accident itself wrote the undo handle as the destination's current catalog entry. Undo = `c4 patch` (read catalog) → `c4 cat <pre-image-id> > pre.c4m` → `c4 patch pre.c4m <dir>`. The undo run records *its* pre-image first, so undo is itself undoable, indefinitely — the log is the undo stack. Restoration is byte-exact and metadata-exact (the snapshot carries mode/timestamp columns).

Surface consequences, all subtractive: `patch -s` (opt-in backup) and `patch -r` (reverse-via-changeset) are **retired** — subsumed by the default plus two existing verbs, and `-r`'s changeset-OldID lookup was incoherent anyway. The only escape hatch is the existing long-form flag with honestly broadened meaning: `--no-store` = write nothing to the store, including the pre-image — destructive, long-form-explicit, no short form, no prompt. `--dry-run` remains the free look. No interactive prompts anywhere in the loop.

## 5. The five tasks as exact compositions

**T1 — recover from store alone** (no new verbs; log default-arg on `patch`):
```
c4 id -s -q project/                    # snapshot; stderr: recorded: c4SNAP…
rm -rf project/                         # lose the tree (and any redirected output)
c4 patch                                # catalog: "- <time> <size> project.c4m c4SNAP…"
c4 cat c4SNAP… > project.c4m
c4 patch project.c4m project/           # byte- and metadata-exact materialization
c4 cat c4SNAP… | c4 id                  # equals: c4 id project/ | c4 id
```

**T2 — undo the accident:**
```
c4 patch release.c4m tools/             # WRONG dir; pre-image recorded first (stderr shows c4PRE…)
c4 patch                                # catalog: "- <time> <size> tools.c4m c4PRE…"
c4 cat c4PRE… > pre.c4m
c4 patch pre.c4m tools/                 # restore; this run records the broken state too
```

**T3 — same content?** (identity default of `c4 id`, spec's own pipe law):
```
machineA$ c4 id src/ | c4 id            # → c4CONTENT…
machineB$ c4 id src/ | c4 id            # → c4CONTENT…   string-equal ⇔ byte-identical
```

**T4 — fast and safe:** `c4 id -s -q assets/` on 20k files ≈ hash/read time + ~2.5 s durability overhead (never per-file full flushes). Guarantees as in §3: mid-command crash → log unchanged, snapshot nonexistent, source untouched; after the `recorded:` line → snapshot and all referenced bytes survive power loss.

**T5 — read the store from one ID:**
```
c4 cat c4SNAP…                          # the description: full listing with metadata
c4 cat c4SNAP… | c4 paths               # bare path list
c4 cat c4SNAP… | grep -F 'report.pdf'   # entry line ends with the file's content ID
c4 cat c4FILE… > report.pdf             # extract; cat verifies bytes hash to ID
c4 cat -r c4CONTENT…                    # given a content ID instead: expand Merkle listings
```

## 6. Budget accounting and rejected alternatives

Concepts: **2** (content ID, snapshot ID — the log rides the existing "history is a patch chain" concept and the existing store). New verbs: **0**. New flags: **0** (two *retired*: `patch -s`, `patch -r`; one long-form flag broadened: `--no-store`; three no-arg defaults added to `log`/`patch`/`gc`; `-x`, `-q`, `--dry-run`, `--no-fsync` unchanged).

Rejected: a `c4 snap`/`c4 restore` verb pair (pure porcelain over `id -s`/`cat`+`patch`; fails the composition test). A plain-text index file of snapshot IDs (new format; the patch chain is an existing concept with existing readers). Keying the snapshot blob by its denoted root content ID (collides with the root's one-level listing object — one key, two byte-objects — and breaks hash-of-bytes verification). A `--content`/`-m c` identity mode (keeps the determinism violation as the default; two IDs competing for one column). Making `c4 id` of a c4m stream return the description's own ID (breaks the spec's `c4 id DIR | c4 id = ID(DIR)` law and T3's one-pipe answer; the store log plus verify-on-read `cat` covers the snapshot-ID recompute need).

## 7. Compatibility notes (non-normative)

Existing stores remain valid (content addressing is indifferent to why an object exists); old statful listing objects are simply additional blobs. Chain readers accept legacy statful checkpoints on input while writers emit content-form only — partial knowledge is a valid state. Concurrent appends to the log serialize via an advisory lock; sections remain the atomic unit.
key_decisions: Directory identity becomes stat-free by default: a directory's C4 ID hashes the one-level canonical listing in content form (mode '-', timestamp '-'), using the spec's first-class null fields — no grammar change, and identical bytes now yield identical IDs on any machine (fixes T3, honors determinism).

Exactly two user-visible identity concepts: content ID (bytes) and snapshot ID (a recorded description's own bytes) — one hashing mechanism, two named roles; a snapshot is just a c4m file stored as content.
The ID a c4m stream denotes (c4 id of stdin/file, diff/patch boundary IDs, chain checkpoints) is its root content ID, making the spec's pipe law 'c4 id DIR | c4 id == ID(DIR)' hold exactly.

Snapshot-with-storage always captures the description: id -s / bare c4 / patch scan paths store the full snapshot c4m at its own ID and append one entry to the store log (founding complaint 1 fixed as a default, zero new surface).

The store log <store>/log.c4m is an ordinary c4m patch chain — one file-entry section per recorded description ('rootname.c4m' + snapshot ID); history, catalog, time-travel, and archiving are the existing log / patch / patch -n / split verbs.
No-argument defaults unify discovery: c4 log, c4 patch, and c4 gc with no c4m named operate on the store log ('when no c4m is named, the store's log is the c4m').

Reconcile records a durable pre-image by default before the first destructive operation (retiring patch -s and patch -r); undo is the log itself — cat the pre-image snapshot and patch it back; undo is undoable because the undo run records its own pre-image.
Destructive opt-out is long-form only: --no-store (existing flag, honestly broadened) skips all store writes including the pre-image; --dry-run remains the free look; no interactive prompts.

Durability protocol from the measured physics: per-object fsync+atomic-rename (~130 microseconds/file), then log append, then ONE full-device flush barrier (~5.4 ms) before the command reports — ~2.5 s overhead for 20k files, never per-file F_FULLFSYNC (~3 min); contract: reported means power-loss-proof, unreported means the log never changed.
Log tail is WAL-disciplined: a section appears completely or not at all; readers ignore a torn final section and the next append repairs it.
c4 cat verifies on read that an object's bytes hash to its ID before emitting — one-command falsifiability for every object class (files, listings, snapshots).
Surface budget spent: 0 new verbs, 0 new flags, 2 concepts; two flags retired and one broadened — the design is net-subtractive.
result.stance: composition-first: every capability is a composition of the existing verbs (id, cat, diff, patch, merge, log, split, paths, intersect, explain, gc) and the frozen c4m grammar; new behavior arrives only as changed defaults of existing verbs plus one store-resident file that is itself an ordinary c4m patch chain readable by the existing chain verbs.

# C4-ID(1)

## SYNOPSIS
`c4 id [-s] [-q] [-e] [-S] [-m s|m|f] [-c guide.c4m] [--exclude PAT] [--exclude-file FILE] <path>...`

## DESCRIPTION
Writes the c4m description of each path to stdout. For a directory, the
description lists the tree with mode, timestamp, size, name, and C4 ID
columns. For a c4m file, writes the normalized description. With piped
stdin, prints a single ID: the ID of the input bytes, or, for c4m input,
the ID of the tree the description denotes.

**Identity.** A file's content ID is the ID of its bytes. A directory's
content ID is the ID of the one-level listing of its direct children with
mode and timestamp null (`-`) — so it depends only on names, sizes, symlink
targets, and children's content IDs, never on clocks or umask. The ID
recorded in a directory entry's ID column is its content ID. To print a
tree's content ID as one line:

    c4 id DIR | c4 id

Two trees have equal content IDs exactly when their contents are
byte-identical.

**Snapshots.** With `-s`, content is stored in the configured store and the
description itself is stored as content — its ID is the snapshot ID — and
one entry is appended to the store log `<store>/log.c4m`. The snapshot ID
is printed in the `recorded:` line on stderr and is listed in the log.
Snapshots are recorded for directory trees and ingested c4m files; storing
a lone file records no snapshot (its ID is its handle).

**Durability.** `c4 id -s` reports only after everything is on stable
media: each object is written to a temporary file, fsynced, and atomically
renamed; the log entry is appended; one full-device flush barrier is
issued; then the `recorded:` line prints and the command exits 0. If power
fails before that line, the log is unchanged and the snapshot does not
exist (any orphaned objects are harmless and collected by `c4 gc`). If
power fails after, the snapshot and every byte it references survive. The
source tree is never written to. Durability overhead is roughly 130
microseconds per file plus one ~5 ms barrier — about 2.5 s extra for
20,000 files.

## FLAGS
```
-s, --store          Store content and record a snapshot in the store log
-q, --quiet          Suppress stdout (the c4m); stderr still narrates
-e, --ergonomic      Pretty, column-aligned output
-S, --sequence       Detect and fold file sequences
-m, --mode MODE      Scan depth: s=structure, m=metadata, f=full (default f;
                     -s requires full)
-c, --continue FILE  Use an existing c4m as a guide (only changed files rehashed)
    --exclude PAT    Glob to exclude (repeatable)
    --exclude-file F File of exclude patterns
```

## EXAMPLES
```
c4 id project/ > project.c4m          # describe a tree
c4 id -s -q project/                  # snapshot into the store, record in the log
c4 id project/ | c4 id                # the tree's content ID (one line)
c4 id < a.bin                         # a file's content ID from raw bytes
```

# C4-PATCH(1)

## SYNOPSIS
`c4 patch [-n N] [-e] [-q] [--dry-run] [--source PATH] [--no-store] [--no-fsync] [-m s|m|f] [<target>] [<dest>]`

## DESCRIPTION
Applies a target state.

```
c4 patch                            Resolve the store log → current snapshot catalog
c4 patch <file.c4m>                 Resolve a patch chain → c4m to stdout
c4 patch <dir>                      Scan dir, store + record snapshot → c4m to stdout
c4 patch <file.c4m> <file.c4m>      Resolve chain → write dest c4m
c4 patch <file.c4m> <dir>           Reconcile dir to match the c4m
c4 patch <dir> <file.c4m>           Scan dir, store + record snapshot, write c4m
c4 patch <dir> <dir>                Reconcile dest dir to match source dir
c4 patch <file.c4m>...              Multi-file chain resolution
```

With no arguments, resolves the store log: one line per snapshotted name,
newest snapshot per name, its ID in the last column. `-n N` resolves any
chain (including the log) as of step N.

**Reconciling records a pre-image first.** Before the first destructive
operation on DEST, the current state of DEST is stored (content, listings,
and its snapshot), recorded in the store log, and made durable with the
same barrier as `c4 id -s`. Only then is DEST modified. If DEST does not
exist or is empty, there is nothing to preserve and nothing is recorded.
A reconcile that changes nothing records nothing.

**Undo.** The pre-image snapshot ID is printed on stderr and is DEST's
current entry in the catalog (`c4 patch`). To undo:

    c4 patch                        # find DEST's pre-image snapshot ID
    c4 cat <snapshot-id> > pre.c4m
    c4 patch pre.c4m DEST/

The undo run records its own pre-image, so undo is itself undoable.

**Durability.** Files are materialized by temp-file + fsync + atomic
rename — a partially written file is never visible under its real name.
One final barrier precedes exit 0: when the command returns successfully,
DEST is on stable media. If power fails mid-command, DEST holds a mix of
old and new whole files; restore either direction (the pre-image via the
log, or re-run the patch). Content pulls from the store, DEST itself, and
any `--source` paths.

stdout is the changeset applied (bare old ID, patch entries, bare new ID);
`-q` suppresses it. Summary and narration go to stderr.

## FLAGS
```
-n, --number N   Resolve to chain step N (1-based; 0 = latest)
-e, --ergonomic  Pretty output
-q, --quiet      Suppress the changeset on stdout
    --dry-run    Print the operation plan to stderr; change nothing, record nothing
    --source P   Additional content source directory (repeatable)
    --no-store   DESTRUCTIVE: write nothing to the store — no pre-image is
                 recorded and the prior state of DEST becomes unrecoverable
    --no-fsync   Do not fsync materialized files (faster; files may be lost
                 on power failure but remain re-materializable from the store)
-m, --mode MODE  Scan depth for directory arguments: s/m/f (default f)
```

## EXAMPLES
```
c4 patch                              # snapshot catalog from the store log
c4 patch -n 4                         # the catalog as of log step 4
c4 patch release.c4m build/           # reconcile build/ (pre-image recorded first)
c4 patch --dry-run release.c4m build/ # plan only
```

## DESCRIPTION
With a C4 ID, retrieves the object from the configured store and writes it
to stdout. Every read is verified: the object's bytes must hash to the
requested ID, or `c4 cat` writes nothing and fails.

A snapshot ID returns the recorded description — the full listing with
mode, timestamp, size, name, and content-ID columns. A directory content
ID returns the one-level listing of its children; `-r` expands directory
entries recursively from the store. A file content ID returns the file's
bytes.

## FLAGS

```
-e, --ergonomic   Pretty-print c4m content
-r, --recursive   Recursively expand directory entries from the store
```

```
c4 cat c4xk7…Wkc > project.c4m        # retrieve a snapshot description
c4 cat c4xk7…Wkc | c4 paths           # list its paths
c4 cat c4dN4…uWz > report.pdf         # extract one file by content ID
c4 cat -r c4mW3…uTz                   # browse a tree from its content ID
```

# C4-LOG(1)

## SYNOPSIS
`c4 log [<file.c4m>...]`

## DESCRIPTION
Lists the sections of a c4m patch chain, one line per step: index, state
ID, and counts. With no arguments, reads the store log `<store>/log.c4m` —
the append-only chain in which the store records every snapshot it
ingests (from `c4 id -s`, bare `c4 <dir>`, and the pre-image taken by
every `c4 patch` reconcile). Resolve the log with `c4 patch` to see the
current catalog, or `c4 patch -n N` for the catalog as of step N.

The log is an ordinary plain-text c4m file. A power failure during an
append can leave a torn final section; readers ignore it and the next
append repairs the file — a section either appears completely or not at
all.

## EXAMPLES
```
c4 log                                # snapshot timeline of the configured store
c4 log /backup/store/log.c4m          # a store given only as a directory
c4 split ~/.c4/store/log.c4m 40 archive.c4m recent.c4m
                                      # archive history before step 41
```

# C4-GC(1)

## SYNOPSIS
`c4 gc [--force] [-v] [<file.c4m>...]`

## DESCRIPTION
Mark-and-sweep the local store: keep every object reachable from the named
c4m roots, collect the rest. Dry run unless `--force`. With no roots
named, the roots are every snapshot recorded in the store log — nothing
reachable from any logged snapshot is ever collected. To let old
snapshots go, archive the log first with `c4 split`, then run `c4 gc`.

## FLAGS
```
    --force     Delete unreferenced objects (default is a dry-run report)
-v, --verbose   List each unreferenced object
```

# The snapshot–store–restore loop as one surface

## 0. The kills, argued

**Kill 1 — undo does not belong to reconcile.** The shipped surface proves the point: today, undoing a bad reconcile requires that you (a) passed `-s` when you destroyed the data, (b) kept the changeset that went to stdout, and (c) know the special incantation `c4 patch -r changeset dir`. The founding accident satisfies none of these — that is *why* it was an accident. The deeper defect is architectural: a backup subsystem running beside a content-addressed store duplicates the store's entire reason to exist (charge 1: does an existing primitive already express this?). If the store is trustworthy enough to restore *from*, it is trustworthy enough to back up *into*; a parallel mechanism (shadow dirs, kept changesets, reverse modes) is opaque to `cat`, invisible to `gc`, unverifiable by rehash — exactly the opaque-backup incumbent c4 claims to sit beside, not become. Counter-attack: "a clonefile backup preserves fidelity a c4m can't (xattrs)." If true, that is a bug in restore's fidelity, and hiding it behind a second restore path violates one-implementation-per-idea; whatever c4m cannot describe, c4 cannot promise anywhere. Counter-attack: "auto-snapshot is slow/polluting." Dedup makes re-ingest of known bytes a `Has()` check; the genuinely new bytes are precisely the bytes about to be destroyed — the ones that must be saved; measured physics puts the worst case at seconds, and `gc` already exists for space. The kill stands: **there is no undo feature.** `patch -r`, `diff -r`, and store-removals `-s` are deleted. Undo is `restore` of the pre-image snapshot that every destructive restore durably creates and prints.

**Kill 2 — the metadata-bearing directory ID is not an identity.** Today a directory's ID hashes its children's mtimes and modes, so identical checkouts on two machines get different IDs — a standing violation of the project's own principle 10 ("IDs must reproduce across machines, umasks, and clocks"). It answers no question: not "same bytes?" (mtimes pollute it) and not "same exact description?" (the c4m text's own ID answers that completely). It is a third identity squatting between two real ones, and it is the sole reason task T3 is impossible today. Killed. A directory's C4 ID is henceforth computed over its one-level canonical listing **in content form** — stat fields null (`-`), names, sizes, and child IDs real — using only the frozen spec's Merkle rule and first-class nulls (the scanner even ships a documented `dirIdentity` seam anticipating exactly this). Counter-attack: "stat-in-ID detects permission drift cheaply." Drift detection is `diff`'s job, field-level and attributable; an ID that changes for a thousand unrelated reasons names nothing. Counter-attack: "existing stored listings invalidate." True; a one-time re-derivation, and verification-over-assertion makes every stale listing falsifiable by recomputation. An identity that fails the determinism principle is the larger debt.

**Kill 3 — "durable-every-write" is the wrong promise, and trees get none.** Physics: per-file F_FULLFSYNC is ~6.4 ms — ~3 minutes for 20k files — to guarantee something nobody can act on ("file 7,214 was durable at t+83 s"). Content addressing already converts corruption into *detection*: any object either rehashes to its name or it is garbage. So durability is promised at exactly one point — the claim. Ingest claims nothing until its log line is on stable media; after that, everything the claim covers is durable. Materialized working trees receive **no durability promise at all**: the store is the system of record, a tree is a projection re-derivable in one command, and pretending otherwise (`patch --no-fsync` as an opt-out of per-file fsync during reconcile) doubles cost and halves honesty. `--no-fsync` dies; materialization never per-file-fsyncs; fast is the default because safe lives in the store. Counter-attack: "store and tree share a disk — 'store of record' is circular." The ingest barrier is on stable media; losing the tree is recoverable; losing the disk is replication's problem, which no fsync policy solves — the promise is scoped so it is never a lie.

**Reframed — snapshots do not auto-store, but storing is never partial.** `c4 id` without `-s` stays a pure function (tree → text); description is a read, archival is a write, and coupling them would make the primitive impure. But the current `-s` is a *half-store*: file bytes go in, the description that makes them meaningful stays out — founding complaint 1 verbatim. The premise that dies is that "store the content" and "store the description" are separable operations. An unstored description leaves stored bytes anonymous; a stored description over unstored bytes is a dangling promise. `-s` becomes total.

## 1. Identity: two concepts, one mechanism

Everything has exactly one kind of name — the C4 ID of some canonical bytes — used in two roles:

- **Content ID** — *what the bytes are.* A file's content ID is the C4 ID of its bytes. A directory's content ID is the C4 ID of the canonical one-level listing of its direct children in content form: mode `-`, timestamp `-`, size real, name real, child content IDs real, link targets kept (a symlink's target string *is* its content). Same bytes ⇒ same content ID on every machine, any umask, any clock. This is *the* identity of a tree; T3 is answered by string equality of two `c4 id -q` outputs.
- **Snapshot ID** — *what was written down.* The C4 ID of a description's canonical text. It pins every recorded observation — mtimes, modes, structure — as well as content. Not a new mechanism (a c4m file is a file; this is its content ID), but a named role because the loop traffics in it: `-s` logs it, `cat` retrieves by it, `restore` restores by it, `gc` roots through it.

Two trees with equal content IDs may carry snapshots with different snapshot IDs (different observed mtimes). Each concept answers exactly one question; nothing answers both, and nothing else is user-visible. Metadata remains fully recorded in c4m entries — as observations, never as identity. Zero grammar changes: the spec's Merkle rule ("directory ID = ID of the one-level canonical listing") and first-class nulls are used exactly as frozen; what changes is only which observation fields enter the identity listing — none.

## 2. Self-description: the store alone recovers everything

`c4 id -s DIR` now performs a **total ingest**, one atomic claim:

1. every file's bytes → object under its content ID (dedup skips existing);
2. every directory's content-form one-level listing → object under its content ID (so any tree ID is `cat`-able and the Merkle walk works store-only);
3. the canonical c4m text itself → object under its snapshot ID;
4. one section appended to the store's log, `<store>/snapshots.c4m`.

The log is an **ordinary c4m patch chain** — the frozen grammar, no headers, nothing new. Each ingest appends one entry plus the chain's bare accumulated-ID boundary:

```
- 2026-07-08T17:31:02Z 623 src.c4m <- abyss:/Users/joshua/ws/demo/src c4UwPu…
c4qPdt…
```

The entry describes a real store object *as a file* (name = label `<basename>.c4m`, size = the description's byte size, ID = the snapshot ID — every field verifiable by `cat` + rehash), timestamped with ingest time (an observation, like any c4m timestamp), with provenance recorded as an inbound flow link (`<- host:/abs/path` — location:path is frozen grammar; the path may contain slashes there, which the name field forbids). Because it is a patch chain, re-snapshotting the same label is a *modification*: `c4 cat` of the log shows the current snapshot per label; `c4 log` of it shows full history — release-history-is-a-patch-chain, literally. The log is the store's only non-content-addressed file (a growing log cannot name itself); it lives at the store root, so "delete everything outside the store" preserves it. `gc` composes unchanged: `c4 gc ~/.c4/store/snapshots.c4m` marks the closure of every logged snapshot.

This closes complaint 1 exactly: there is no way to store a tree without storing its description, and the description is discoverable from the store alone (T1), while `c4 cat <id>` lists any snapshot or tree and fetches any file byte-exactly (T5) with zero new surface.

## 3. Durability: logged ⇒ durable; trees are projections

**Ingest protocol** (local store): write objects via the existing temp + `fsync(2)` + rename writer (~126 µs/file; no torn object is ever visible under its final name); **barrier 1** — one device flush (F_FULLFSYNC on the store root, ~5.4 ms) makes all object bytes stable; append the log section and `fsync(2)` it; **barrier 2** — second device flush makes the claim stable; only then exit 0 (and only then does `restore --force` print the pre-image ID and begin destruction). Invariant: **a logged snapshot is a durable snapshot; exit 0 means logged.**

Power loss mid-command: the prior store is untouched (puts are create-only; dedup skips); unlogged new objects are inert, harmless garbage — `gc` collects them, re-running is idempotent; a torn final log line means the ingest never claimed success — log readers recover to the last valid boundary and warn on stderr. Any doubt about any object is falsifiable in one pipe: `c4 cat <id> | c4 id -` either prints `<id>` or the object is garbage.

**Cost (T4):** 20,000 files ingest in seconds — hashing at storage bandwidth, ~2.5 s of per-file `fsync(2)`, plus ~11 ms of barriers. The ~3-minute per-file-F_FULLFSYNC regime is explicitly not used because it purchases nothing the claim-point promise doesn't already give.

**Materialization:** `restore` writes files via atomic rename with *no* per-file fsync (~112 µs/file; readers never observe partial files) and makes **no power-loss promise for the tree**. Exit 0 means: the tree matches the target *now*, and both endpoints — pre-image and target — are durable snapshots in the store. Power loss during or just after a restore is recovered by re-running the same command; nothing is lost because nothing recoverable ever lived only in the tree. (S3/multi-store: the claim point is the backend's acknowledged write; the log lives in the first — write — store.)

## 4. Destructive reconcile: one tree-writer, safe by default, undo as a consequence

**`c4 restore TARGET DIR` is the only verb that writes working trees.** `patch` returns to pure c4m algebra (chain resolution to stdout); its seven-way dispatch, directory modes, `-r`, `--dry-run`, `-s`, `--no-fsync`, and `--source` are deleted. The accident class "patch ate my directory" becomes unconstructible: patch cannot touch a directory at all, and the verb that can is safe twice over.

- TARGET is always a *description*: a `.c4m` file, a 90-char C4 ID (snapshot ID for full fidelity; tree content ID restores byte-exact content with null metadata → defaults — partial knowledge degrading gracefully), or `-` for stdin. A directory is never a target: dir→dir mirroring is the pipeline `c4 id -s A | c4 restore - B`, so "which side wins" can never be confused again — the description side, always.
- **Default is a dry run.** stdout is the exact changeset that `--force` would apply, in the frozen patch format: bare current-state ID, entries, bare target ID. Empty output = already matching. Nothing is written. And by construction the plan's first bare line *is* the pre-image snapshot ID that `--force` will print — the plan literally reads "from OLD to NEW."
- **`--force`** (the single new flag; long-form-explicit, precedent `gc --force`): validate the plan and content sources (missing content aborts *before* anything else); take a complete full-fidelity pre-image snapshot of DIR through the total-ingest protocol above — **durable, logged, before the first destructive operation**; print the pre-image snapshot ID to stdout; reconcile; narrate a summary plus the literal undo command on stderr. If DIR is missing or empty the pre-image is the empty description — its constant ID is still printed and logged, keeping stdout uniform for scripts.
- **Undo (T2)** is therefore not surface: `c4 restore --force <printed-pre-image-id> DIR`. The accident's own output is the antidote; the undo is itself undoable (it prints *its* pre-image), snapshots all the way down, every one discoverable in the log, verifiable by rehash, collectable by gc. There is no opt-out flag for the pre-image: the case where it is expensive (a large unsnapshotted tree) is exactly the case it exists for, dedup makes the repeat case cheap, and users who truly want capture-free destruction already own `rm -rf`.

## 5. Surface accounting

Budget: **2 identity concepts** (content ID, snapshot ID) · **1 new verb** (`restore`) · **1 new flag** (`--force` on restore) · 0 grammar changes · 0 dependencies · stdout byte-pure everywhere (dry-run plans and pre-image IDs are data on stdout; counts, timings, undo hints are stderr; `c4 explain restore` narrates).

One existing flag is redefined, not added: `id -q` now prints only bare content IDs (root tree ID for a directory; a c4m file's own canonical ID — its snapshot ID — for a c4m), matching the established stdin behavior of printing a bare ID. Deleted surface: `patch` loses six flags and four argument forms; `diff` loses `-r`/`-s`/`-q`; the interactive store-creation prompt is replaced by an error naming the fix (no prompts in composable verbs). Net flag count falls by roughly seven. One well-known file appears: `<store>/snapshots.c4m`, in the frozen format.

## 6. Task closure

- **T1**: `c4 id -s src > src.c4m`; `rm -rf src src.c4m`; `c4 cat ~/.c4/store/snapshots.c4m` → read snapshot ID; `c4 restore --force <id> src`; `c4 id -q src` matches. Store-alone, byte-exact.
- **T2**: wrong-dir `restore --force` prints pre-image ID and the undo command; one command restores byte-exact (content and recorded metadata), verified by `c4 id -q`.
- **T3**: `c4 id -q <checkout>` on each machine; string-equal content IDs iff byte-identical, regardless of mtimes/umask.
- **T4**: seconds for 20k files; exit 0 ⇒ snapshot logged and durable; interruption ⇒ prior store intact, partial work inert or falsifiable, re-run idempotent; restored trees carry no durability promise — re-run restore.
- **T5**: `c4 cat <snapshot-or-tree-id>` lists; `c4 cat <file-id> > name` extracts; `c4 cat <id> | c4 id -` verifies.

The loop closes with the store as the single durable truth, two identities that each answer one question, a log that is itself the format it protects, and an undo story that was never a feature — only a consequence.
