key_decisions: KILL: undo-as-a-subsystem is deleted (patch -r, diff -r, store-removals -s, kept changesets); the default pre-image snapshot of every destructive restore IS the undo, and its ID is the command's stdout

KILL: the stat-tainted directory ID dies; directory C4 IDs hash the one-level canonical listing in content form (stat fields null, per frozen null machinery), so identical bytes give identical tree IDs across machines (T3 by string equality)

KILL: durable-every-write and tree durability; durability is promised only at the claim point — objects fsync'd, one device barrier, log line fsync'd, second barrier, then exit 0 — so 'logged implies durable'; materialization never per-file-fsyncs (--no-fsync deleted) and restored trees carry no power-loss promise (re-run restore)

REFRAME: id stays pure (no auto-store), but -s becomes a total ingest — file bytes + directory listings + the canonical description itself + one log line — storing content and description are never separable
Exactly two user-visible identities, one mechanism: content ID (what the bytes are; files and trees) and snapshot ID (the C4 ID of a description's canonical text, pinning recorded metadata)

The store self-describes via <store>/snapshots.c4m — an ordinary c4m patch chain (frozen grammar): one entry per snapshot with label, ingest time, size, inbound flow-link provenance (host:/path), and snapshot ID; c4 cat = current, c4 log = history, c4 gc <log> = root set
restore is the ONLY verb that writes working trees; patch returns to pure chain algebra (its 7-way dispatch and 6 flags deleted), making the original accident unconstructible
restore's target is always a description (c4m file, ID, or stdin '-'), never a directory; dir-to-dir mirroring is the pipeline `c4 id -s A | c4 restore --force - B`
restore defaults to a dry run whose stdout is the exact changeset in frozen patch format, and the plan's first bare ID line equals the pre-image ID that --force will print

--force is the only new flag: validate sources, ingest the pre-image durably BEFORE any destruction, print the pre-image snapshot ID to stdout, reconcile, narrate the literal undo command on stderr; no opt-out flag for the pre-image
id -q is redefined (not added): print bare content IDs only — root tree ID for a directory, a c4m file's own snapshot ID — matching the existing bare-ID stdin behavior

Restoring a tree content ID degrades gracefully (null metadata → umask/current-time defaults); restoring a snapshot ID reproduces recorded times and modes, closing the byte-exact round trip (a re-scan of a restored tree reproduces the same snapshot ID)
T4 physics: 20k files ingest in seconds (~126µs/file plain fsync + two ~5.4ms barriers); the ~3-minute per-file F_FULLFSYNC regime is rejected as buying an unusable promise

points.point: Budget arithmetic is the headline argument: the brief allows <=1 verb and <=2 flags, and this design spends 0 and 0 — and then goes negative by retiring `patch -s` and `patch -r`. Exactly 2 named identity concepts, 0 grammar changes, 0 dependencies. Every rival design now carries the burden of justifying surface this candidate proves unnecessary. It is the project's founding aesthetic made literal: 'the best feature proposals turn out to already be possible' — the audit found the pieces 90% present, and the design is the missing coherence, not missing machinery.

Content ID as the default directory identity is a bugfix, not a redesign. Today's stat-hashing IDs violate the project's own determinism principle ('IDs must reproduce across machines, umasks, and clocks') and make T3 structurally unanswerable. The fix stays entirely inside the frozen spec: the Merkle rule is untouched; the null fields the grammar already makes first-class pin WHICH canonical listing is hashed. Every surviving field — name, size, symlink target, child content IDs — is a pure function of bytes. Nothing is lost: mode and timestamp move to the recorded description's columns, where mutable facts belong. One sentence teaches it: identity is bytes; metadata is record. And it preserves the spec's own composition law exactly — `c4 id DIR | c4 id` prints ID(DIR) — which is T3's whole answer in one pipe.

The store log is the entire self-description mechanism, and it is NOT a new structure: `<store>/log.c4m` is an ordinary c4m patch chain, so `log`, `patch`, `patch -n N`, and `split` already read it. Timeline, current catalog, time-traveled catalog, and archival all arrive as dividends of one file placement plus one default-argument rule — 'when no c4m is named, the store's log is the c4m' — which teaches three verbs in a single sentence. That sentence is precisely what a cold LLM agent driving the CLI from --help needs: it extends knowledge the agent already has (chains) rather than adding knowledge it must discover.

Founding complaint 1 is answered at its root, not its symptom. A hash cannot embed itself, so the description's ID must live in an external structure — and the design picks the doctrinally correct one: a sidecar of immutable content IDs (the log), not a header (grammar-frozen), not a special object class, not a database. Storing the snapshot c4m as content at its own hash means the description IS content, closing the 'content survives but metadata is lost' gap by construction. T1 closes with zero bytes retained outside the store: catalog → snapshot ID → `cat` → `patch`, byte- and metadata-exact.

Founding complaint 2 is answered by reordering, not adding. Reconcile already guided-scans DEST to compute its changeset; the pre-image is that same scan fed through the existing ingest path before the first destructive operation, made durable with the same barrier. Dedup makes it near-free exactly when the reconcile is routine, and expensive only when DEST holds unknown bytes — which is precisely the wrong-directory accident, the one case where the cost is the rescue. The undo handle is written BY the accident and surfaces as DEST's current catalog entry (top of `c4 patch` output, under DEST's own name). Undo is itself a reconcile, so undo records its own pre-image: the log is an undo stack by construction, not by feature. 'The flags for the backup solution' are not promoted to defaults — they are deleted, because the default subsumes them.

The durability contract is stated in the only vocabulary a user can observe: 'if the command reported the snapshot (or exited 0), power loss loses nothing — snapshot, referenced content, and log entry all survive; if power failed earlier, the log is unchanged and the snapshot does not exist.' Two outcomes, no fsync trivia. It is grounded in the measured physics, not aspiration: per-object fsync (~126µs) plus ONE device barrier (~5.4ms) ≈ 2.5s overhead on 20k files, versus the ~3min per-file F_FULLFSYNC path the design explicitly bans — and the transcript's 9.8s wall clock for 20,143 files is consistent arithmetic from those numbers. Orphaned objects from an interrupted run are harmless by content addressing and sweepable by `gc`. Materialization mirrors it: temp+fsync+rename means no torn file is ever visible; mid-command loss leaves a mix of old and new WHOLE files, recoverable in either direction because the same run already made the pre-image durable. That last clause is why `--no-fsync` is safe to keep offering.

Two nouns, one mechanism. Content ID and snapshot ID are both hash-of-bytes — a directory listing's bytes ARE the canonical listing text, so listing-ID and blob-ID coincide — which yields one uniform falsifiability rule: `c4 cat` verifies every read against the requested ID and refuses to emit otherwise. File blobs, Merkle listings, and snapshot descriptions all get 'verification over assertion' from a single sentence of documentation and zero special cases.

The rejected-alternatives section does real analytic work rather than taste-signaling: keying the snapshot blob by its denoted root content ID provably collides (one key, two distinct byte-objects — the root's one-level listing and the full description) and breaks hash-of-bytes verification; a `-m c` identity mode keeps the determinism violation as the default and puts two competing IDs in one column, destroying T3's cold-user string-equality answer; a snap/restore verb pair is pure porcelain over `id -s` and `cat`+`patch`. Each rejection is a proof of minimality for the element that survived.

The acknowledged pipe-law asymmetry is the correct trade, and its strongest form should be stated affirmatively: `c4 id` of a c4m yields the DENOTED tree ID because the spec's composition law and T3's one-pipe answer outrank local symmetry. Snapshot-ID recomputability does not suffer: the canonical encoding is deterministic (sorted, canonical fields, byte-identical on every machine given the same recorded fields), so re-ingesting the same description re-mints the identical snapshot ID, and verify-on-read `cat` checks the binding on every retrieval. No stored ID is ever trusted, only checked — the falsifiability requirement is met without bending the pipe law.

Torn-tail handling is a reader-tolerance policy on exactly one file, not a grammar change: an unclosed final section is already legal in the frozen chain format, and the log merely narrows that to 'a malformed final section is ignored and repaired by the next append.' Section-level append atomicity is what upgrades the log from a convenience file into the load-bearing source of truth for the durability contract — the snapshot 'exists' if and only if its section is complete, which is the same fact the two-outcome power-loss contract rests on.

Beside, not instead — the design does exactly what each incumbent structurally cannot. git: per-repo and committed-only, and its hashes bake in history and metadata, so it can never answer T3's cross-machine 'byte-identical?' by string equality; content ID can. Backup tools: opaque archives; here the description is plain text, greppable (T5 is literally `grep -F 'report.pdf'`), diffable, and readable by the existing verbs. Harness checkpoints: session-local and tool-blind; the store log survives sessions and records pre-images no matter which tool caused the mutation. And stdout stays byte-pure throughout — catalog and changesets are data; `recorded:` lines and reconcile summaries are stderr narration — demonstrated end-to-end in an actual transcript, not asserted.

Fix (flag accounting, stated once and unambiguously): new flags introduced = 0; flags retired = 2 (`patch -s`, `patch -r`); existing long-form flag broadened = 1 (`--no-store` now honestly means 'write nothing to the store, including the pre-image'); no-argument defaults added = 3 (`log`, `patch`, `gc`). The `--no-store` broadening is the design's only escape hatch and it lands precisely on 'destructive by long-form-explicit': no short form, no prompt, self-describing help text that names the consequence ('the prior state of DEST becomes unrecoverable').

Fix (synopsis consistency): the --help excerpt writes `c4 cat [-e] [-r] <c4id|path>` while C4-CAT(1) writes `<c4id | file.c4m>`. The man page form is correct — cat retrieves store objects by ID or displays a c4m file — and the excerpt should match it verbatim so a cold agent sees one grammar, not two.

Fix (compress the patch case table into one invariant): every directory argument to `c4 patch` is recorded as a snapshot before it participates — as source, so the changeset's boundary IDs are always resolvable from the store later; as destination, as the pre-image. Stating this as a single rule replaces two paragraphs of case analysis with an invariant a cold user can predict unseen combinations from, and it explains why `c4 patch <dir>` and `c4 id -s` deliberately converge rather than accidentally overlap.

Log hygiene is the right economics and should be defended as such: only descriptions are logged (never raw blob puts — `echo x | c4` cannot spam the catalog), absent/empty DEST records nothing, a no-op reconcile records nothing. The log therefore stays a catalog of meaningful states, `gc`'s default roots ('every snapshot in any log section') stay meaningful, and forgetting remains an explicit composition — `split` the log, then `gc --force` — never a retention policy. GC-by-default can never silently collect history, which is the safe-by-default rule applied to time.

result.target_stance: composition-first: every capability is a composition of the existing eleven verbs (id, cat, diff, patch, merge, log, split, paths, intersect, explain, gc) and the frozen c4m grammar; new behavior arrives only as changed defaults of existing verbs plus one store-resident file that is itself an ordinary c4m patch chain readable by the existing chain verbs

points.point: The unification thesis is the design's spine and the strongest answer to the brief's demand for ONE coherent surface: all four questions collapse into a single mechanism — a content-addressed store trusted with everything, including its own descriptions. Undo is restore of a pre-image snapshot; self-description is the description stored as an ordinary object plus one log line; durability is a single claim point; identity is one naming rule (C4 ID of canonical bytes) in two roles. Each sub-answer is a consequence of the others rather than four features stapled together — exactly the project's chartered aesthetic that new power must arrive as a consequence of the existing design. No competing shape achieves this: any design that keeps a separate backup mechanism, a third identity, or per-file durability necessarily answers the four questions with four disjoint mechanisms.

Kill 1 is the verbatim, maximal-honesty reading of founding complaint 2. 'We built flags for the backup solution — it needs to be the default' is not a request to re-default a flag; it is evidence the flags were the defect. Today's undo requires three opt-ins (-s at destruction time, a kept changeset, knowledge of patch -r) that the accident user by definition never made — an undo path that exists only for people who foresaw the accident protects no one. Making the pre-image an unconditional, durable, logged prerequisite of destruction is the minimal design under which the accident class cannot exist; anything weaker re-admits the founding accident. And the architectural argument seals it: a backup subsystem running beside a content-addressed store duplicates the store's entire reason to exist, and is opaque to cat, invisible to gc, unverifiable by rehash — the opaque-backup incumbent c4 claims to sit beside, not become.

No opt-out on the pre-image is correct, not overreach. The case where the pre-image is expensive — a large, never-snapshotted tree — is precisely the case where it is saving unique bytes about to be destroyed: cost is proportional to irreplaceability, which is the right proportionality for a safety mechanism. Dedup reduces the repeat case to a Has() sweep (seconds by measured physics), gc already owns space reclamation, and capture-free destruction remains fully available as rm -rf — so no capability is removed from the system, only a footgun from this verb. An opt-out flag would exist solely to reconstruct the founding accident.

Kill 2 is not a format change and does not spend the zero-format-change budget: it is the design question's own stated invitation ('the spec's null fields permit a stat-free identity') executed with zero grammar delta. The frozen Merkle rule (directory ID = ID of the one-level canonical listing) and first-class nulls are used exactly as frozen; the only change is which observation fields populate the identity listing — none — an implementation choice behind the scanner's documented dirIdentity seam. It is also the only move that makes T3 answerable by string equality within the two-concept budget: retaining the stat-tainted ID either fails T3 outright or forces a third user-visible identity concept. The stat-tainted ID answers no question the two real identities don't answer better, and it stands in open violation of the project's own determinism principle. Migration cost is a one-time re-derivation of stored listings, and verification-over-assertion makes every stale listing falsifiable by recomputation — a bounded debt retired against an unbounded one.

Two identities is the theoretical minimum, not a chosen pair. The brief's tasks require distinguishing 'same bytes?' (T3) from 'which exact record, metadata included?' (T1/T2 fidelity restore), and no single ID can answer both, because two machines legitimately record different observations of byte-identical trees. Content ID and snapshot ID are the same mechanism — the C4 ID of some canonical bytes — in two roles, so the design introduces zero new naming machinery, each concept fits the mandated one sentence, and metadata remains fully recorded in c4m entries as observations that never enter identity. Drift detection correctly moves to diff, where it is field-level and attributable, instead of an ID that changes for a thousand unrelated reasons and therefore names nothing.

Kill 3 replaces an unusable promise with an actionable one and answers T4 with measured numbers rather than vibes. 'File 7,214 was durable at t+83s' is a promise no caller can act on; 'exit 0 implies logged implies the entire snapshot including its description is durable' is one bit a script can branch on. The barrier order — all object bytes stable via one device flush BEFORE the log line is flushed by a second — guarantees a durable claim never references unstable objects: the write-ahead invariant with the data ahead of the claim. Cost: ~2.5s of per-file fsync(2) plus ~11ms of barriers for 20k files, versus ~3 minutes for the per-file F_FULLFSYNC regime that promises strictly less. Power-loss semantics are total: prior store untouched (puts are create-only), unlogged objects inert and gc-collectable, torn final log line recovers to the last valid chain boundary, re-run idempotent.

Sharpening: the retained per-file fsync(2) is not residual durability theater — it is what makes put-by-ID idempotent after a crash. fsync-before-rename ensures any object visible under its final name is complete, so dedup's Has() remains a valid skip-check on re-run; without it, a torn object could sit under its final name and be silently trusted by every future ingest. ~126 microseconds per file is the exact minimal price of 'presence implies integrity,' and integrity stays independently falsifiable in one pipe: c4 cat <id> | c4 id -. State this rationale explicitly in the design; it converts an apparent inconsistency (why fsync at all if durability lives at the claim point?) into a load-bearing invariant.

'Trees are projections, no durability promise' is honesty, not weakness. Any per-file-fsync promise for a working tree still dies to the shared-disk case, so the design scopes the promise to what fsync can actually deliver and states the recovery path plainly: re-run the same command; nothing recoverable ever lived only in the tree, because both endpoints of every forced restore — pre-image and target — are durable snapshots before the first destructive operation. This is verification-over-assertion applied to durability semantics themselves: the promise is scoped so it is never a lie. Deleting --no-fsync removes a flag whose only function was to let users opt out of a promise that was already unkeepable.

The total-ingest reframe answers founding complaint 1 at the level of ontology, not workflow. It identifies 'store the content' and 'store the description' as one indivisible act, because each is meaningless without the other: an unstored description leaves stored bytes anonymous; a stored description over unstored bytes is a dangling promise. Simultaneously, id without -s stays a pure function (tree to text, nothing written anywhere), preserving the read/write separation that a CLI driven cold by LLM agents needs to be safe to explore — description is a read, archival is a write, and the design refuses to couple them while refusing to split the write. stdout byte-identical with and without -s means -s is composable into any existing pipeline with zero behavioral surprise.

The snapshot log is the design eating its own cooking, and it is the provable minimum of fixed-point machinery for T1. The store's one non-content-addressed file — honestly stated, with the honest reason: a growing log cannot name itself — is an ordinary c4m patch chain in the frozen grammar. Therefore cat gives current-snapshot-per-label, log gives full history, split gives retention, gc takes it directly as a root set, any text tool reads it, and every field of a log entry (name, size, timestamp, provenance flow link, snapshot ID) is independently verifiable by cat plus rehash. Even crash recovery of a torn final line falls out of the chain's existing boundary lines. Re-snapshotting a label being a chain modification makes 'release history is a patch chain' literal. T1's store-alone recovery reduces to exactly one well-known filename.

restore as the single tree-writer with description-only targets makes the founding accident unconstructible rather than merely survivable — a strictly stronger safety class. patch returns to pure c4m algebra and cannot touch a directory at all; 'which side wins' cannot be confused because the description side always wins and a directory is never a target; dir-to-dir mirroring is an explicit pipeline (c4 id -s A | c4 restore --force - B) that states its own direction. The default dry run's first bare line IS the pre-image snapshot ID that --force will print — the plan literally reads 'from OLD to NEW,' and scripts get one uniform contract: first line of the plan equals stdout of --force, uniform even for a missing or empty directory via the constant empty-description ID. A cold agent driving from --help cannot destroy anything without typing --force, and the moment it does, the antidote is printed in the output it just received. Undo is itself undoable, snapshots all the way down, all discoverable in the log — T2 closed by consequence, not by feature.

Surface accounting is net negative while capability strictly grows — the fewest-concepts budget enforced as an outcome, not a promise. Within budget: 1 new verb (restore), 1 new flag (--force, with gc --force precedent for long-form-explicit destruction), 2 identity concepts, 0 grammar changes, 0 dependencies. Deleted: patch loses six flags and four argument forms, diff loses three flags, the interactive prompt becomes an error naming the fix; net flag count falls by roughly seven. The redefined id -q is a redefinition, not an addition, and it aligns with the established stdin behavior of printing a bare ID. Against incumbents the positioning holds exactly as chartered: works on any directory (git is per-repo and committed-only), transparent and rehashable (backup tools are opaque), tool-agnostic and durable across sessions (harness checkpoints are session-local and tool-blind).

Fix (small self-inconsistency): make explicit that in the content-form listing a directory's size field is content-derived — the sum of its descendants' byte sizes — never st_size. The transcript already implies this (testdata/ shows size 1112, equal to its sole child cases.txt), but st_size for directories is filesystem-dependent and would silently re-taint the content ID that Kill 2 just purified. One sentence in the IDENTITY section closes the hole.

Fix (cosmetic self-inconsistencies): (a) the illustrative log block's boundary line reuses cases.txt's ID (c4qPdt...) — a placeholder typo; the boundary is the chain's accumulated-state ID and should read as such. (b) State in id(1)'s output documentation that the 'stored snapshot ... in 0.6s' line is stderr narration — the transcript already proves it (stdout was redirected into src.c4m and is byte-identical with and without -s), but the man page should say it so the byte-purity guarantee is explicit rather than inferred.

Out-of-scope pressure is pre-answered with existing algebra, which is itself evidence the representations were chosen correctly. Pre-images accumulating in the log is GC policy — a stated non-goal — and when that work arrives, retention is already expressible as patch-chain algebra (split to truncate, log to audit) composed with gc taking snapshots.c4m as the root set. Likewise multi-store and remote backends inherit the claim-point semantics unchanged (the claim point is the backend's acknowledged write). No future mechanism is mortgaged; the design leaves every deferred question answerable with verbs that already exist.

The print barrier is the minimal correct answer to the whole brief because it is the strengthening of an act every possible design must perform anyway: printing the ID. The brief asks for four features (identity, self-description, durability, undo); this design supplies one sentence — 'an ID is printed only after everything it transitively names is durable in the store, and any printed ID is recoverable from the store alone' — and derives all four. stdout becomes a transaction commit record: for the brief's first-class cold LLM agent, the entire mental model fits in the two lines of --help footer ('printed = safe; unprinted = nothing happened'), which no ref system, journal, or snapshot registry can match for teachability. Nothing smaller exists, because a design that prints IDs without this guarantee must add a second artifact to carry recoverability — and that artifact is exactly what founding complaint #1 shows users losing.

The 'found unification' is not a design conjecture — it is shipped code. WriteCanonical (/Users/joshua/ws/active/software/c4/oss/c4/c4m/manifest.go:105-155) provably renders only minimum-depth entries and skips nested directory lines, so the canonical ID of a tree's description EQUALS the root directory's frozen Merkle ID. The snapshot object therefore already exists as ordinary store content; the only gap producing complaint #1 was that the root's one-level listing was never stored and its ID never printed. The fix is two behaviors (store the root listing; print its ID), zero new object kinds, zero format changes — the strongest possible instantiation of the workspace's founding principle that 'the best feature proposals turn out to already be possible.' Every rival design that mints a snapshot artifact, ref, or header is adding a concept the frozen grammar already expresses.

Content mode is an anticipated seam, not a retrofit: /Users/joshua/ws/active/software/c4/oss/c4/scan/generator.go:65-70 defines dirIdentity with the comment 'the seam for alternate canonicalizations (e.g. a future content mode hashing null-stat entry lines): install a different function, nothing else in the walk changes.' The codebase predicted this exact design. So T3's defect (mtime-polluted directory IDs) is cured by a null-projection of the ONE existing identity mechanism — content ID and snapshot ID are two knowledge levels of the same Merkle rule, not two identity systems. That lands exactly on the 2-concept budget with each concept genuinely one sentence, and the field split is principled, not arbitrary: size is a function of the bytes (stays), mode varies with umask (nulled — T3 names umask), timestamp varies with clocks (nulled). The content ID is falsifiable anywhere by recomputation; the tool never asserts sameness it did not compute.

Undo is structurally self-insuring, which strictly exceeds complaint #2's ask. The complaint demanded backup-by-default; this design makes backup the MEANING of the destructive verb: line 1 (the victim's snapshot ID) is printed only after the prior state is fully durable and always before the first mutation. There is no flag to forget, no flag to disable, no trash directory, no reflog, no new state — undo is the same verb reading its own output, and redo falls out free because the undo prints the mistake's ID as ITS line 1. The pre-image costs nearly nothing (the scan is the same scan reconcile needs; dedup stores only missing bytes). And because the operation is invertible, dropping confirmation ceremony is correct, not cavalier: 'safe by default' is satisfied by construction rather than by prompt.

The durability protocol is measured, dominated, and honestly two-sided. Per-file F_FULLFSYNC (~6.4ms x 20k = ~3min) buys nothing over fsync(2)-per-file plus ONE end-of-run device barrier (~2.5s + 5.4ms) given temp-file+atomic-rename and self-verifying object names: a torn object is detectably invalid, treated as absent, and healed by an idempotent rerun. The T4 answer is therefore the strongest form possible — 'printed implies the closure survives power loss one microsecond later; unprinted implies the source tree was never touched, the store is consistent, and rerun continues where it left off' — every clause checkable. Deleting --no-fsync is right because 'fast by flag' is satisfied by having made safe fast (126us/file); a mode would multiply crash states for zero benefit. The fsync code already exists in the safety-defaults worktree (store/fsync_darwin.go, store/sync.go) — this is staged engineering, not aspiration.

The surface accounting is uniquely subtractive and under budget on every axis: +1 verb (restore, justified because no existing verb materializes trees), 0 new flags against an allowance of 2, net -7 flags by returning patch to pure text algebra, 2 concepts against an allowance of 2, 0 grammar changes, 0 dependencies, 0 flags on restore itself. Narrowing patch does not merely guard the accident vector of complaint #2 — it deletes it, and the error message teaches the correct command ('patch composes descriptions; to change a directory: c4 restore'). This is 'one implementation per idea' enforced at the CLI: the reconcile engine gets exactly one face, and preview is composition (c4 diff <dir> <target>) rather than a --dry-run mode — dry-run isn't deleted, it's what pure patch always outputs now.

Store homogeneity makes T1 and T5 hold by construction and makes the store's meaning outlive the binary. Exactly two object kinds exist — user bytes, and human-readable one-level listing text — both plain files named by their own IDs. With the tool lost, a shell recovers everything (find the file named by the ID, read the listing, follow the last field). Falsifiability is one pipeline (cat -r ID | recompute = same ID, guaranteed by the flatten rule). And Merkle sharing of listing objects gives O(changes) snapshot history — a history mechanism with no history feature, no refs, no 'latest' pointer, keeping naming outside the store where git, shell history, and lockfiles already do it well ('beside, not instead').

The empty description as a universal fixed point eliminates every edge case in one move, and the constant is real: c459dsjf...c1sFT is the verified C4 ID of zero bytes (/Users/joshua/ws/active/software/c4/oss/c4/id_test.go:26). It is the pre-image of an absent target (line 1 when <dir> didn't exist), the way to empty a directory undoably, and the reason a no-op restore prints the same ID twice — three would-be special cases collapse into ordinary resolution of one always-resolvable ID.

Against the named incumbents the positioning is exact: git snapshots committed state per-repo (and cannot answer cross-machine 'byte-identical?' for an arbitrary directory in one string comparison); backup tools are opaque (fail plain-text/diffable/falsifiable); harness checkpoints are session-local and tool-blind. This design checkpoints ANY directory, uncommitted state included, into a store whose every object a human or agent can read, verify, and diff — doing what the incumbents structurally cannot, never re-doing what they do.

Sharpen one transcript spelling to remove a latent ambiguity: the verification one-liner should be `c4 cat -r ID | c4 id -q -`, not `c4 cat -r ID | c4 -x`. Rule stated crisply: bare `c4` on stdin identifies raw bytes (frozen shortcut, unchanged); `c4 id ... -` parses stdin as a description. This keeps stdin handling deterministic (no content-sniffing, which would violate 'determinism everywhere') while preserving the identical round-trip guarantee via the flatten rule. Strictly a spelling fix; no surface change.

State the legitimacy of the default changes in one sentence rather than defensively: redefining -s to print only the snapshot ID is not collateral churn — the old behavior (dump the whole manifest to stdout) printed precisely the losable artifact of complaint #1, so the old default WAS the bug; and `-m c` as the id default fixes the founding T3 defect at the moment the crucible exists to fix defaults before freezing. Grammar, the 90-char ID, and the Merkle rule change zero; the breaking changes are confined to flag output conventions, the cheapest layer to change and the most expensive to leave wrong.

GC composes without a retention concept: undo handles are ordinary roots kept by keeping their IDs, and restore's two-line byte-pure stdout feeds existing gc's explicit-roots interface directly (e.g. append lines to a roots file). The non-goal stays a non-goal, but the seam is already load-bearing — evidence the one-property design closes over future policy questions rather than deferring them.

result.target_stance: Subtractive-minimal — the store is the design: one property (the print barrier: an ID is printed only after everything it names is durable in the store, and any printed ID is recoverable from the store alone) carries identity, self-description, durability, and undo; surface change is +1 verb, 0 new flags, net -7 flags, 2 identity concepts, 0 format changes.

points.point: Data loss by composition of two documented behaviors: `c4 id -s file.bin` stores a lone file but 'records no snapshot (its ID is its handle)', while `c4 gc` with no roots uses 'every snapshot recorded in the store log' as its root set. The deliberately stored lone file is reachable from no logged snapshot, so the next `c4 gc --force` — run exactly as documented, to clean up — silently deletes content the user explicitly asked the store to keep. The safety default (log-derived roots) and the ingestion rule (lone files unlogged) ship as a loaded gun. Either the root rule or the no-snapshot-for-files rule must change after freeze.

The snapshot ID — one of the two paid-for identity concepts — is not user-recomputable, violating 'every claim recomputable; a stale record must be falsifiable in one command.' Per C4-ID(1), piping c4m-shaped bytes into `c4 id` yields the DENOTED tree ID, never the bytes' own ID, so no surface command can compute or verify a snapshot ID from a c4m file in hand; falsification is delegated entirely to store-side `cat` verify-on-read. Worse, which identity `c4 id` assigns to stdin depends on whether the bytes happen to parse as c4m — a parse heuristic silently selects between two different IDs for `c4 id < a.bin`. Fixing requires new surface (e.g. a bytes-mode flag) after freeze.

The catalog and the documented undo path are keyed by basename: log entries are `- <time> <size> <rootname>.c4m <snapshot-id>` and C4-PATCH(1) says undo begins 'find DEST's pre-image snapshot ID' in `c4 patch` output. Any two trees sharing a basename (~/a/tools vs ~/b/tools, ubiquitous names like src/, build/, tools/) collide; the catalog shows only the newest, so the sanctioned undo flow hands the user the WRONG pre-image and `c4 patch pre.c4m tools/` then destroys data via the safety feature itself (it does record a pre-image of that destruction, but the user believes they restored). The log-entry schema is load-bearing store metadata; adding a path/disambiguator after stores accumulate logs is a migration — must change before freeze.

The single most important machine datum of `c4 id -s` — the snapshot ID — is emitted only in the stderr `recorded:` narration line (transcript confirms; with `-q` stdout is empty). The project's own principle declares stderr non-machine, so a script or LLM agent automating T1 must either scrape narration or fall back to the collision-prone basename catalog lookup. The operation produces two data (description + its ID) but the design gives the second no byte-pure channel, despite 2 of 2 flags in the budget sitting unspent. As shipped this must change after freeze.
points.principle: 9 — stdout is data, stderr is narration

points.point: `--no-store` is broadened from its verified current meaning ('Suppress content storage', oss/c4/cmd/c4/patch.go:23 — benign store hygiene) to 'no pre-image is recorded and the prior state of DEST becomes unrecoverable.' Every existing script using the flag for its shipped meaning silently loses the safety net the entire design exists to provide. 'Destructive by long-form-explicit' means the user explicitly types the danger — inheriting destructiveness into a previously benign shipped flag is the opposite of explicit. It also welds two orthogonal choices together: you cannot skip content ingest while keeping the pre-image. A new dedicated long-form flag was affordable (0/2 flag budget spent).

`c4 patch` becomes an 8-way dispatch on argument type-sniffing: bare = catalog, one c4m = resolve, one dir = scan+store, c4m→c4m = write file, c4m→dir = reconcile, dir→c4m = snapshot, dir→dir = reconcile, N c4ms = multi-chain. Semantics flip on filesystem state, trailing slash, and (presumably) the .c4m extension — a dest path that doesn't exist is either 'a c4m file to write' or 'a tree to materialize' with no stated rule; a directory literally named data.c4m breaks dispatch entirely. Founding complaint 2 was verbatim 'I got the usage wrong' — the candidate preserves the exact confusable positional surface and compensates with pre-images rather than removing the confusion. Fewest concepts means fewest MEANINGS per verb, not fewest verb names.

`c4 patch <dir>` (single arg) is a second spelling of `c4 id -s <dir>` — the same snapshot+store+record idea implemented under two verbs, which the charge sheet's principle 12 bans on sight. It additionally makes an exploratory-looking invocation mutating: a cold user 'seeing what patch does' to a directory ingests gigabytes into the store and appends a log entry, with no dry-run default on that path.

The identity migration is underplayed and institutionalizes two identity computations forever. Every existing store, c4m file, diff boundary ID, and chain checkpoint carries statful directory IDs that the new content-form rule invalidates for verification; §7's answer — 'chain readers accept legacy statful checkpoints on input' — means a verifier must try TWO rules per directory ID indefinitely, and 'falsifiable in one command' becomes 'falsifiable under either of two rules.' Mixed-version reality breaks T3 silently: machine A on the new binary and machine B on v1.0.13 report different IDs for byte-identical trees and the user concludes the content differs. No verify/migrate story is surfaced. (The stat-free identity itself is invited by the design question and is not the count; the permanent dual-acceptance and absent migration story are.)

The durability contract is platform-overfit to APFS physics. 'One full-device flush (F_FULLFSYNC on the log fd)' as a barrier covering all prior object writes and renames is a macOS-specific semantic; Linux has no single-fd whole-device barrier, and rename durability there requires fsync of each containing directory (the sharded store touches many). Yet C4-ID(1) states the power-loss promise unconditionally ('if power fails after, the snapshot and every byte it references survive'). T4's fixed success task demands saying 'precisely what is guaranteed' — the precise answer differs by platform and the surface hides that. The promise as written must be weakened or the protocol changed post-freeze on non-APFS targets.
points.principle: 7 — claims must hold when checked (and 10 — across machines)

points.point: log.c4m acquires a private parse dialect: 'a malformed final section is dropped' is reader behavior special-cased to one file location, so identical bytes parse differently depending on where they live. Copy the log to archive it (`c4 log /backup/store/log.c4m` is a documented invocation) and torn-tail handling is ungoverned — error, silent drop, or silent data difference. Plain text as THE universal interface forbids context-dependent readers; the grammar either tolerates malformed final sections everywhere (a de facto grammar change, budget: zero) or nowhere.
points.principle: 2 — plain text is the universal interface (and 10)

points.point: The only sanctioned way to shrink the store — 'split the log, move the recent half into place, gc --force' — is an unlocked read-modify-write race against the advisory-lock append protocol. A snapshot recorded by a concurrent `c4 id -s` in the window between split-read and mv loses its log entry; default-root gc then collects its content. The one recipe documented for forgetting has a data-loss race, in a design whose founding complaint is accidental destruction.

SUCCESS TASK T1/T2 (cold user): the recovery entry point is undiscoverable and mis-signaled. The --help excerpt documents patch as 'c4 patch [flags] <target> [<dest>] — Apply target state' with <target> looking required; nothing in --help says bare `c4 patch` is a read-only catalog listing. A cold user (or a cautious LLM agent, the declared first-class user) will not run an apparently mutating verb with no arguments to READ state — the fact appears only mid-man-page in a dispatch table. The designated first command of both T1 and T2 recovery flows is invisible from the top-level surface, and running a 'patch' verb to merely look violates the safety signaling the verb taxonomy exists to provide.
points.principle: 8 / 4 — safe defaults, porcelain documents its composition

points.point: Budget laundering in §6. Claimed spend: 2 concepts, 0 verbs, 0 flags. True spend: 2 identity concepts + 2 more load-bearing user nouns ('the store log' with its own path, torn-tail rule, and lock protocol; 'the catalog' with per-name resolution semantics — the docs use 'catalog' as a term of art the user must learn) + 3 new no-arg modes (log/patch/gc) + 1 new single-arg patch shape + 1 flag semantically converted to destructive + 2 shipped flags retired + 1 file-specific parser dialect. Principle 1's budget covers ALL concepts, not only the ones labeled 'identity'; 'the log rides an existing concept' does not make 'when no c4m is named, the store's log is the c4m' free — the design itself admits it takes a sentence to teach.

Retiring shipped flags is a breaking change presented as 'subtractive': `patch -r/--reverse` exists in the shipped v1.0.13 CLI (verified at oss/c4/cmd/c4/patch.go:20) and `-s` is referenced in its own error text (patch.go:456). Existing scripts break. Defensible pre-1.x, but the candidate should say 'breaking removal', not book it as budget credit.

SUCCESS TASK T5: given 'one ID and the store only', the two ID concepts are indistinguishable by inspection (both 90-char c4…), and `c4 cat` of a file content ID dumps raw — potentially 4.8 GB of binary — to the terminal with no way to ask first. `c4 explain` exists precisely as the human-narration verb and is left unwired to the store; extraction of 'one named file' is grep-plus-hand-copying a 90-char ID because `c4 paths` emits paths without IDs. Completable, but only by a user who already guesses the ID's kind correctly.
points.principle: 9 / 4 — explain is the human verb; composition should cover the task

points.point: Partial knowledge is unhandled by the identity story: the grammar makes null size and null ID fields first-class, but the denoted content ID of a description containing null child IDs or sizes is undefined — C4-ID(1) is silent on whether `c4 id` of a partial c4m errors, degrades, or fabricates. A design that repositions nulls as the foundation of content identity (mode/timestamp nulled) owes an answer for the other nullable columns.
points.principle: 11 — partial knowledge is a valid state

result.target_stance: composition-first: every capability is a composition of the existing eleven verbs and the frozen c4m grammar; new behavior arrives only as changed defaults of existing verbs plus one store-resident file that is itself an ordinary c4m patch chain

points.point: The undo story is self-contradictory at its root set, and the contradiction freezes. The snapshot log keys entries by basename label ('src.c4m'), and 're-snapshotting the same label is a modification' — so snapshotting ~/projA/src then ~/projB/src evicts projA's snapshot from the log's current view. The candidate then claims BOTH that 'c4 gc <store>/snapshots.c4m marks the closure of every logged snapshot' (history as roots — then no pre-image is ever reclaimable and the repeated answer ''gc already exists for space'' is void) AND that gc is the space remedy (current-state roots, per the frozen patch-chain resolution semantics — then every label-collided or superseded pre-image, i.e. the undo mechanism itself, becomes collectable garbage, and 'durable before destruction' expires at the next gc --force). Whichever root rule ships is the safety contract; the candidate ships both and would have to break one after freeze.

The undo promise is asserted, not recomputable — by the candidate's own argument. C4-RESTORE(1) UNDO promises 'restores <dir> byte-exact to its state before the restore, including recorded metadata,' but the pre-image is a c4m snapshot and the FROZEN grammar has no vocabulary for xattrs, ACLs, ownership (uid/gid), hard-link topology, fifos, or files the user can't read. Kill 1's own maxim — 'whatever c4m cannot describe, c4 cannot promise anywhere' — convicts this man page. The one mechanism that met the promise (whole-tree clonefile: measured 0.26s for 14k files, full fidelity) was killed on purity grounds. Founding complaint 2's 'quietly destroyed' recurs one level down: the accident-user's ownership and xattrs are silently destroyed under a banner of safety, and the fidelity boundary appears nowhere on the surface.

Deleting patch --source makes the store a mandatory middleman for every dir-to-dir operation. restore pulls content only 'from the configured store and from bytes already present in <dir>' — so mirroring A into B REQUIRES total-ingesting A (a full byte copy of A into the store) first. For this product's core workload (multi-hundred-GB media trees) that doubles every transfer's writes and permanently grows the store as a side effect of a copy. The obvious cold pipe 'c4 id A | c4 restore --force - B' (no -s) fails on missing content — a trap the man page never names. An existing primitive (reconcile with a directory content source) expressed this capability; the candidate deletes it and offers nothing in its place. Re-adding it later spends the last flag in the budget.

The '-q redefinition' is a silent byte-output flip of a shipped machine-facing flag, hidden from the surface accounting. Today -q means 'Suppress output (useful with -s)' (verified: cmd/c4/id.go:21). Under the candidate, every existing 'c4 id -s -q' silent-ingest script starts emitting 90-char IDs on stdout — precisely the class of break 'byte-identical output' forbids — and no quiet mode remains at all. Calling this 'redefined, not added' is a third surface expenditure dressed as zero; the budget arithmetic (1 verb + 1 flag) is only true if you don't count breaking a flag as spending one.

One flag, two identities: 'c4 id -q src.c4m' prints the CANONICALIZED text's ID (snapshot ID) while 'c4 id - < src.c4m' prints the raw bytes' ID — same file, two different answers from the same verb, dispatched by content sniffing. If the on-disk c4m is not already canonical (e.g. saved from -e ergonomic output), the two IDs differ and there is NO way to obtain a c4m file's plain content ID via -q. The candidate's own creed — 'each concept answers exactly one question; nothing answers both' — is violated at the exact flag that anchors T3, and a cold user has no way to know which question -q just answered.

Kill 2 retroactively invalidates every directory ID ever shipped, with no coexistence surface. All existing c4m files, patch chains, constellations, and stored listings carry stat-tainted directory IDs that stop verifying under the null-form rule; 'c4 cat <old-tree-id>' dangles. Worse, T3 across a mixed-version fleet silently answers 'different content' for byte-identical trees — and the fixed 90-char ID carries no marker of which rule computed it, so string equality cannot falsify the wrong answer; verification-over-assertion is defeated by design. 'A one-time re-derivation' is asserted in one clause and never designed: no verb, no flag, no migration story. (The kill itself is invited by the brief; the missing transition is the count.)

snapshots.c4m is the store's only mutable, non-content-addressed file, and its write path is unspecified exactly where the durability invariant lives. Two concurrent 'c4 id -s' runs (or a 'restore --force' pre-image landing during another ingest) interleave appends to one shared file with no stated locking or ordering — 'byte-identical output at any concurrency' has no answer here, and 'logged => durable' depends on an append+fsync being atomic across processes. The candidate's own S3 aside ('the log lives in the first write store') names a backend where append does not exist. Every store replicator and sync tool must now special-case the one file T1 depends on — the log decorates the store rather than standing beside it.

The dry-run output spec contradicts itself: DESCRIPTION defines the plan as 'bare current-state ID, entries, bare target ID' (and the transcript's dry run prints boundary IDs even when creating from empty), while OUTPUT states 'Empty output means <dir> already matches.' Under the stated format a matching dir must emit two bare boundary lines, not nothing. Scripts keying on emptiness and scripts parsing boundaries will disagree; one sentence must change after freeze.

The budget's only verb is spent on a rename, not a capability. 'Apply a description to a working tree' already existed as patch's directory mode; safe-by-default could have been retrofitted in place — dry-run default plus --force, with exact precedent already shipped in gc (cmd/c4/gc.go:18) — for zero new verbs. The candidate's justification (patch returns to pure algebra) has genuine value, but honest accounting says restore re-expresses an existing primitive and the verb budget bought naming clarity.

The retained '-m s|m|f' scan modes are unreconciled with the new stat-free identity. Either 'id -q -m s' (structure scan) prints a content ID computed from bytes it never hashed — an assertion, not a verification — or content IDs become scan-mode-dependent, giving one tree multiple 'content IDs.' The man page documents the flag and says nothing; a determinism hazard sits unresolved directly on the flag surface of the identity the whole design pivots on.

Success-task T1 (recover from store alone), cold-user count: recovery hinges on knowing the magic path <store>/snapshots.c4m plus manual store-root resolution. The short 'c4 --help' never mentions the log; it lives in one FILES stanza of the id man page ('$C4_STORE, or the store line(s) in ~/.c4/config, or ~/.c4/store'). 'Store line(s)' is plural with no rule for which store's log '-s' appends to or which log cat/restore consult in a multi-store config. No verb enumerates snapshots. A careful reader completes T1; a cold LLM agent driving from --help alone plausibly stalls at 'where is the description?'.

Full-fidelity snapshot text is no longer line-locally verifiable for directories. A snapshot renders child entries with real stat fields, but embeds directory IDs computed over the invisible null-form ('content form') transform of those same lines — a canonicalization convention taught nowhere on the surface. 'c4 cat <id> | c4 id -' verifies the stored listing object, but from the snapshot text alone a directory entry's ID cannot be recomputed from the lines the reader is looking at. That is a third, unnamed format concept (the content-form listing) hiding inside the claimed two-identity budget.

result.target_stance: CONTRARIAN — kills undo-as-subsystem (undo = restore of a durable pre-image snapshot), kills the stat-tainted directory ID (null-form content ID), kills per-write durability (claim-point 'logged => durable', trees are projections); reframes -s as a total ingest (bytes + listings + description + log line); adds `restore` as the sole tree-writer, dry-run by default, `--force` long-form.

points.point: IDENTITY DISPATCH IS HEURISTIC AND UNPINNED — the same bytes get different IDs depending on filename and a content sniff, and the design freezes IDs without pinning the rule. Shipped evidence the candidate inherits: helpers.go:215 dispatches on `.c4m` extension OR looksLikeC4m(); looksLikeC4m (helpers.go:166-177) fires on ANY file whose first non-blank line starts with '-', 'd', 'l', 'p', 's', 'b', or 'c' — e.g. a Markdown bullet list. Worse, id.go:250-268 shows scan-time ingestion CANONICALIZES any child file that merely parses as c4m and REWRITES its recorded C4 ID (`if newID != entry.C4ID { entry.C4ID = newID }`), so a snapshot of an ordinary tree stores different bytes than the tree contains; restore materializes the canonicalized text, and the 'verify by recomputation' step passes anyway because canonicalization is idempotent — silently certified corruption. This falsifies T1's 'byte-exact' and the print-barrier property ('any printed ID is recoverable') for a class of ordinary trees. The man page's own verification recipe `c4 cat -r ID | c4 -x` works only if bare c4 sniffs stdin as c4m (otherwise it hashes the expanded multi-level text, not the root listing), yet `echo data | c4` must hash bytes — the surface never says which. Also unpinned: the ID of a patch-chain c4m (resolve first?) and whether `c4 id -q file.c4m` vs byte-identical `file.txt` may legally differ. Every one of these choices changes printed IDs, the exact artifact being frozen.

'THE PRIOR STATE IS ALWAYS RECOVERABLE' IS FALSIFIED BY THE DESIGN'S OWN NULL SEMANTICS. Principle 11 makes a partial scan a valid state, and the shipped scanner already behaves that way: id.go:245-247 `continue // skip files we can't open` — ingestion silently skips unreadable files and prints the snapshot ID anyway. Apply that to restore's pre-image: a victim directory containing an EPERM file, socket, or fifo yields a pre-image with null/absent entries; reconcile then DELETES bytes the store never received; line 1 cannot resurrect them, yet the man page promises the absolute. The design must either abort on incomplete knowledge (contradicting 'never demand completeness', and nowhere stated on the surface) or weaken the frozen guarantee — either way the frozen man-page semantics change. Same hole on the snapshot side: `c4 id -s` on a partially readable tree prints an ID whose restore is silently not byte-exact (T1 fails without any error). Aggravation: restore — the only verb that can empty an arbitrary directory in one command with zero flags — has no dry-run default, contradicting principle 8's literal text ('dry-run defaults'; gc obeys it); the sole justification is an invertibility this count shows has holes.

THE UNDO HANDLE LIVES ONLY ON EPHEMERAL STDOUT; THE STORE CANNOT NAME ITS OWN ROOTS (prosecutes T2). Refs, journal, and registry were removed as a virtue, so the ONLY copy of the pre-image ID is line 1 of one process's stdout. No surface verb enumerates stored snapshot/listing roots — `log` lists patches in a chain, gc's dry run lists garbage, `cat` needs the very ID that was lost. A script with `>/dev/null`, a crashed agent harness, or lost scrollback, and the 'always recoverable' state is unreachable-by-name forever. The founding complaint-#2 user — who by definition got the usage wrong — is precisely the user least likely to have captured line 1. T2 completes from the surface only under the unstated assumption that stdout survived the accident. 'The store ALONE recovers everything' is true only given a name the store alone cannot supply.

GC'S EXISTING SURFACE CONTRADICTS RESTORE'S FROZEN PROMISE. Pre-image snapshots are, by design, reachable from no c4m file the user holds — they exist only as store roots named by discarded stdout lines. The first `c4 gc --force project.c4m` therefore collects the entire undo history that restore's man page calls 'always recoverable', silently. GC *policy* is a declared non-goal, but an absolute guarantee on one man page that an already-shipped verb falsifies is not policy, it is a contradiction between two frozen surfaces; neither man page warns, and the candidate's only nod ('undo handles are roots you keep by keeping their IDs') is buried in the design essay, not the user surface a cold user reads.

CONCEPT ACCOUNTING: 'TWO IDENTITY CONCEPTS' UNDERCOUNTS A FOUR-VALUED AXIS PLUS THREE SMUGGLED AXIOMS. The `-m s/c/m/f` axis mints four distinct legal canonical listings — four distinct IDs — for the same tree, all reachable via `-q`; the docs name two points on the axis and hope users never land on the others. `-m m` yields an identifiable description containing no IDs at all: an identity principle 7 can never check against content. Unbudgeted concepts presented as 'not a concept, an argument convention': (a) the ID-or-path resolution rule on every verb, (b) the always-resolvable empty-ID axiom — a special case declared adjacent to the words 'no special cases', embodied as a 90-char magic constant in the man page, (c) the print barrier itself, which users must internalize to reason about durability. Real ledger: +1 verb, +1 mode value, 2 redefined flags, 1 redefined bare invocation, ~5 concepts. Still lean — but the claimed arithmetic is advocacy, not accounting.

BARE `c4 <path>` INGESTS BY DEFAULT WHILE `c4 id <path>` DOES NOT — the identical operation has opposite defaults depending on whether the user typed the verb. A cold user (or agent reading --help top-down, where the shortcut appears as a first-class usage line) asking 'what is this tree's ID' via `c4 proj/` silently writes potentially gigabytes into C4_STORE; the cheap action hides behind `-x`. That is 'safe by default, fast by flag' inverted: the expensive, state-creating action is the default and the free one is flagged. It is also a second implementation of `id -s` as an unnamed default verb (principle 12), and if `-x` is new surface the claimed '+0 flags' is false. Defaults freeze with 1.0; if this trap is wrong it changes post-freeze.

T5 BEYOND THE TOP LEVEL IS NOT COMPLETABLE FROM THE SURFACE ALONE. Listing works (`c4 cat <id>`), but extracting a NESTED named file requires knowing the line shape of `cat -r` output — bare names vs full paths is specified nowhere in --help or either man page (only a NOTE inside the patch man page mentions cat at all). The extraction recipe (grep the name, take the last 90-char field, `c4 cat <fileID> > name`) appears only in the transcript, which is not part of --help. The existing primitive that already expresses this — `c4 paths`, the c4m-to-path-list converter — is never connected to store reading by any surface text. A cold agent will succeed at the top level by pattern-matching the listing, and stall one directory down.

SILENT SEMANTIC REVERSAL OF `-q` AND `-s` BREAKS THE SUITE'S OWN STDOUT COVENANT. `-q` flips from print-nothing to print-90-bytes; `-s` flips from print-whole-manifest to print-one-ID. Every existing pipeline of the form `c4 id -s dir > snap.c4m` now writes a bare ID string into a file named .c4m — a file whose subsequent treatment falls straight into the unpinned dispatch of count 1 (is an ID-containing .c4m a description? an ID reference? garbage?). Pre-freeze breakage is legal, but a suite whose creed is 'stdout is data' owes redefined output contracts an explicit migration note; the surface has none.

BOUNDARY DISHONESTY IN THE UNDO ALGEBRA. The pre-image of an ABSENT directory is defined as the empty ID, so undoing a restore-into-absent-dir yields an existing empty directory, not absence — the round-trip claim of byte-exact state restoration overstates by one inode, in the exact edge case (`dir created if absent`) the verb itself advertises. Separately, concurrent restores to one directory have no stated semantics — two agents interleaving create/remove against the same tree — despite LLM agents being declared first-class users; 'safe for the store' (put-by-ID, atomic rename) is asserted, but nothing is said for the tree.

# c4 snapshot–store–restore — Merged Draft v1 (Judge's synthesis)

## Verdict shape

The merge keeps candidate A's *found unification* (the canonical text of a description flattens to the root's one-level listing, so a description's own ID and the root directory's ID are the same mechanism at the same knowledge level), candidate C's *safety posture* (restore is the sole tree-writer, dry-run by default, `--force` long-form, unconditional durable pre-image), and candidate B's *store journal* (an ordinary c4m patch chain inside the store), with the convicted parts of each removed. Two properties carry the whole design:

1. **The print barrier.** A snapshot ID reaches stdout only after everything that ingest stored — file bytes, listings, and the journal entry — is on stable media. Printed means durable; unprinted means nothing was claimed, the source tree was never written to, the store's prior contents are intact, and rerun is idempotent (dedup skips existing objects).
2. **The journal.** The store names its own roots. Every `-s` ingest (including every pre-image taken by `restore --force`, including single files and stdin blobs) appends one section to `<store>/log.c4m`, an ordinary c4m patch chain. `c4 log` with no arguments lists it. This is what rescues the complaint-#2 user whose scrollback is gone, and what closes complaint #1's deepest form ("the ID itself is also losable").

## 1. Identity — one mechanism, two named knowledge levels

There is exactly one naming rule (frozen): the C4 ID of canonical bytes; for a directory, the bytes are the one-level canonical listing of its direct children. The design pins *which observation fields populate the listing* — a semantics choice the frozen grammar's first-class nulls already permit — and names the two levels users need:

- **content ID** — listing with mode and timestamp null; names, sizes, symlink targets, and child *content* IDs real. Equal iff contents are byte-identical, on any machine, clock, or umask. Default for `c4 id`. Answers T3 by string equality.
- **snapshot ID** — listing with everything observed (modes, times too); directory entries carry child *full-listing* IDs, so every ID in a full listing is line-locally recomputable from the object it names (this resolves the "invisible transform" count against C). Printed by `c4 id -s`; the recovery handle.

Directory size field = total bytes of contained files in both forms (deterministic; never st_size). A single file's snapshot ID and content ID coincide (its bytes). By the flatten rule, a description's own canonical-text ID equals its root ID at its own level — so the pipe law (`c4 id DIR | c4 id -q -` prints DIR's content ID) and snapshot-ID recomputability (`c4 id -q saved.c4m` reprints the snapshot ID; `c4 cat -r SNAP | c4 id -q -` verifies round-trip) are the *same* rule, answering B's "snapshot ID not recomputable" blocking count without breaking the pipe law.

**Dispatch is pinned, no sniffing** (answers A's blocking count 1): a top-level argument ending in `.c4m`, and `-` on `id`, parse as descriptions (unparseable `.c4m` argument = error, never silently hashed); every other file argument is bytes; **files inside a scanned tree are always bytes** — never parsed, never canonicalized, never re-ID'd (kills the id.go:250-268 silent-corruption class; T1 byte-exactness depends on it). Bare `c4` with piped stdin identifies raw bytes. Patch chains resolve to their final state before identification (`patch -n` reaches earlier states).

## 2. Self-description — the store alone recovers everything

`c4 id -s DIR` is a total ingest: file bytes; per-directory full-form listings (the snapshot graph, root included); per-directory content-form listings (the content graph, so content IDs also resolve via `cat`/`restore`); one journal section. Listings are tiny text objects; both graphs dedup across snapshots (unchanged subtrees reuse objects — O(changes) history with no history feature). There is no separate "description blob" (B's separate-blob model rejected: it minted a second object kind and a key-collision hazard; under the flatten unification the description *is* the root listing). Ingesting a description (`c4 id -s x.c4m`, `c4 patch chain | c4 id -s -`) stores its listings; the surface states plainly that referenced content is not thereby stored — partial knowledge is first-class, and `restore` pre-flights the closure.

Journal semantics: **history only**. Each section is one entry line (`- <UTC time> <listing size> <name>.c4m <- <host:abs-path> <snapshot ID>`) plus the chain boundary. B's "resolve the log as a current catalog keyed by name" is rejected outright — basename collisions handed the user the wrong pre-image (B blocking / C blocking) — and with it goes bare-`c4 patch`-as-catalog (undiscoverable, mis-signaled). Discovery is `c4 log` (the verb literally named for it), which lists every section, evicting nothing. Torn tails: writers hold an advisory lock and repair (truncate) an incomplete final line before appending; readers of any c4m warn on stderr at trailing garbage — uniform error behavior, not a location-specific dialect, so B's "private parse dialect" count dissolves with zero grammar change.

## 3. Durability — printed means durable; measured, not aspirational

Protocol: objects land temp-file + fsync(2) + atomic rename (~126 µs/file; presence under a final name implies integrity, keeping dedup's Has() valid after a crash); one device flush barrier; journal append + fsync; second barrier; then the ID prints and exit 0. Per-file F_FULLFSYNC is rejected (measured ~6.4 ms/file, ~3 min per 20k files, buys nothing over the claim-point barrier). 20,000 files: hash-bound seconds plus ~2.5 s of fsync and ~11 ms of barriers — the transcript's 6.1 s is consistent arithmetic. The user contract is stated platform-neutrally ("on stable media", "one device flush barrier"); APFS/M-series figures are cited as measurements, and the Linux implementation supplies the equivalent (fsync of files and containing directories / syncfs) — answering B's platform-overfit count without weakening the promise.

Materialization gets the strong, cheap promise (A) rather than none (C rejected as under-promising when 126 µs/file makes the claim nearly free): restored files are written temp+fsync+rename; the target ID prints only after the tree is **verified by recomputation at the target's knowledge level** and one barrier completes. Between restore's two output lines, the tree may hold a mix of old and new whole files — both endpoints are already durable in the store; re-run to finish or restore line 1 to go back. `--no-fsync` is deleted everywhere.

## 4. Destructive reconcile — one tree-writer, plan by default, pre-image before destruction

`c4 restore <target> <dir>` is the only verb that writes working trees. `patch` returns to pure text algebra and errors on directory arguments with a message that teaches `restore` (B's 8-way dispatch and `patch <dir>`-as-second-spelling-of-`id -s` rejected under principles 1 and 12; the accident's grammar is deleted, not merely survived).

- **Default is a dry run** (C wins over A's zero-flag always-apply): principle 8's literal text, the shipped `gc --force` precedent, and the founding "I got the usage wrong" user all favor showing the plan first; A's "invertibility needs no ceremony" was falsified by its own pre-image completeness holes. Plan output is pinned: current-state ID, differing entries, target ID — boundary lines always present, equal IDs and no entries when already matching (fixes C's empty-output self-contradiction).
- **`--force`** (the single new flag): pre-flight the closure (missing content ⇒ list on stderr, exit 1, touch nothing); take a full-fidelity pre-image snapshot of `<dir>` through the total-ingest protocol — durable and journaled **before the first destructive operation**; print the pre-image snapshot ID as stdout line 1; reconcile; verify; print the target ID as line 2. Undo is `c4 restore --force <line 1> <dir>`; redo falls out because the undo prints the mistake's ID as *its* line 1. No opt-out flag exists; B's broadening of `--no-store` into a destructive meaning is rejected (silent destructiveness inherited into a benign shipped flag), and `rm -rf` remains the honest spelling of capture-free destruction.
- **Completeness gate** (resolves A's blocking count 2): `--force` refuses, listing offenders, if `<dir>` contains entries the pre-image cannot fully capture (unreadable files, sockets/fifos/devices) — destruction demands complete capture; description alone stays partial-friendly (`id` warns, records null IDs, exits 2 on partial scans). The **fidelity boundary is stated on the surface**: descriptions record names, sizes, modes, mtimes, symlink targets, hard links, sequences, and content IDs — not ownership, xattrs, ACLs, or special files (C's honesty count adopted; a sidecar can carry more later).
- Absent/empty `<dir>` ⇒ pre-image is the empty description (real constant, ID of zero bytes), still printed and journaled; undo of a restore-into-absent-dir yields an existing empty directory — stated honestly, restore never deletes `<dir>` itself. Concurrent restores of one directory are uncoordinated (store stays safe; tree outcome undefined) — pinned in NOTES.
- Targets are always descriptions (ID, `.c4m`, or `-`); a directory is never a target. Mirroring is `c4 restore --force $(c4 id -s A) B` and the missing-content trap of skipping `-s` is named in the man page. `--source` is rejected for v1 (no success task needs it; store-mediated transfer is the architecture; same-volume clonefile ingest is ~free at measured 0.26 s/14k files; one flag of budget headroom is deliberately preserved — revisit only on measured pain).

**GC coherence** (closes A's gc-eats-undo count and C's root-set contradiction): `gc` default roots = every ID appearing in **any** journal section — full history, both listing graphs, and their closures; explicit c4m arguments **add** roots, never replace. Nothing journaled is ever collectable until the journal itself is explicitly truncated (`split`, then `gc --force`). Retention policy remains a non-goal.

## Surface accounting (honest)

Within budget: **2 identity concepts** (content ID, snapshot ID); **1 new verb** (`restore`); **1 new flag** (`--force` on restore; 1 of 2 spent). Not new flags but real surface, ledgered: mode value `c` on existing `-m` (new default); `id -q`/`id -s` output redefinitions (breaking, pre-freeze, deliberate: the old `-s` printed exactly the losable artifact of complaint #1); bare `c4 <path>` becomes read-only `id` (A's silent-gigabyte trap removed) and stdin no longer auto-stores (`| c4 -s` stores); one well-known file `<store>/log.c4m` in the frozen format; no-arg default on `log`. Deleted: `id -x`; `patch -s/-r/-q/--dry-run/--source/--no-store/--no-fsync/-m` and all directory forms; `diff -r/-s/-q`. Net flag count falls by roughly nine. 0 grammar changes; 0 dependencies; stdout byte-pure everywhere (IDs and c4m text on stdout; counts, undo hints, warnings on stderr; `c4 explain` narrates).

## Migration notes (design-level, not on the user surface)

Legacy stat-bearing listings remain valid store objects and now read as ordinary full-form listings — they verify as the hash of their own text; nothing dangles. Legacy c4m files' directory-ID columns are full-form IDs; content IDs are re-derived in one command (`c4 id -q`). Mixed-version fleets answer T3 only when both ends run the suite that ships content-default IDs — the suite releases together (RELEASE.md), and this identity default is the launch gate.

## Task closure

- T1: `SNAP=$(c4 id -s proj/)`; destroy tree and outputs; if the ID is lost, `c4 log` re-supplies it; `c4 restore --force SNAP proj/` rebuilds byte-exact with metadata, verified before line 2 prints.
- T2: the accident's own stdout line 1 (or `c4 log`) names the victim's pre-image; one `restore --force` returns it byte-exact; undo is itself undoable.
- T3: `c4 id -q dir` on each machine; string-equal iff byte-identical.
- T4: ~6 s for 20k files; printed ⇒ snapshot, content, and journal entry survive power loss; unprinted ⇒ tree untouched, store consistent, rerun resumes.
- T5: `c4 cat SNAP` lists one level; `-r` expands; grep the name, `c4 cat <fileID> > name` extracts; `c4 cat -r SNAP | c4 id -q -` falsifies or confirms in one pipe.

## Open (non-blocking)

Journal-surgery retention recipe's concurrency (stop writers during `split`; gc holds the append lock while rooting) — implementation detail under a declared non-goal. Exact `c4 log` column layout — cosmetic, may adjust after sims. Fidelity sidecar for xattrs/ownership — future external structure per the sidecar doctrine. Journal semantics for non-local (e.g. s3) stores — networking is a non-goal; this surface claims local stores only.

C4-ID(1)

NAME
    c4 id - describe files and directories as c4m text; snapshot with -s

SYNOPSIS
    c4 id [-q] [-s] [-m s|c|m|f] [-e] [-S] [--exclude GLOB]...
          [--exclude-file FILE] [-c GUIDE] <path>...
    c4 id [-q] [-m MODE] -          (parse stdin as a c4m description)

DESCRIPTION
    Writes a plain-text c4m description of each path to stdout. Without
    -s, id reads only; nothing is written anywhere.

    With -s, id also stores a complete snapshot in the configured store:
    every file's bytes, every directory's one-level listing (root
    included, at both full and content detail), and one entry in the
    store journal. stdout is then a single line: the snapshot ID,
    printed only after everything stored is on stable media.

MODES (-m)
    s  structure   names only (no IDs)
    c  content     names, sizes, symlink targets, IDs computed from
                   bytes alone; mode and timestamp null (-). Default.
    m  metadata    modes, times, sizes, names (no IDs)
    f  full        everything observed
    -q requires a mode that records IDs (c or f). -s always records
    full detail and conflicts with -m.

IDENTITY
    A file's content ID is the ID of its bytes. A directory's ID is the
    ID of the one-level canonical listing of its direct children; with
    stat fields null this is its content ID (identical on every
    machine); with observed modes and times it is a snapshot ID. In a
    content-form listing, directory entries carry child content IDs; in
    a full-form listing, child full-listing IDs — every ID in a listing
    is the ID of the exact text of the object it names. A directory's
    size field is the total bytes of the files it contains. A single
    file's snapshot ID and content ID coincide: the ID of its bytes.
    The ID of the empty description (and of zero bytes) is
    c459dsjfscH38cYeXXYogktxf4Cd9ibshE3BHUo6a58hBXmRQdZrAkZzsWcbWtDg5oQstpDuni4Hirj75GEmTc1sFT

DESCRIPTIONS AS INPUT
    An argument ending in .c4m, and `-`, are parsed as descriptions;
    a .c4m argument that does not parse is an error. All other file
    arguments are bytes. Files inside a scanned tree are always treated
    as bytes, whatever their name — never parsed or rewritten. A patch
    chain given to id resolves to its final state first (use
    `c4 patch -n N` for earlier states).

    For a description, id computes at the description's own level of
    detail, so its printed ID is the description's own canonical ID
    (for a full description, its snapshot ID). -m c projects a fuller
    description down to content form; fields cannot be added, only
    nulled. Ingesting a description with -s stores its listings; it
    does not store content the description refers to.

FLAGS
    -q, --quiet          Print only the C4 ID, one line per path
    -s, --store          Snapshot into the store and print the snapshot
                         ID (implies -q)
    -m, --mode MODE      Scan detail: s, c, m, f (see MODES)
    -e, --ergonomic      Column-aligned output
    -S, --sequence       Detect and fold file sequences
    --exclude GLOB       Exclude pattern (repeatable)
    --exclude-file FILE  File of exclude patterns, one per line
    -c, --continue C4M   Use an existing c4m as a scan guide

DURABILITY
    If the snapshot ID printed, the snapshot — content, listings, and
    its journal entry — survives power loss, even one microsecond after
    printing. If it did not print, nothing was claimed: the scanned tree
    was never written to, the store's prior contents and journal are
    intact, and re-running the same command continues where it left off
    (objects already present are skipped). Objects are written to a
    temporary name, synced, and atomically renamed; a device flush
    barrier precedes the journal entry and a second precedes the printed
    ID. Overhead is roughly 130 microseconds per file plus two ~5 ms
    barriers (measured on an Apple-silicon APFS SSD): a 20,000-file tree
    snapshots in seconds.

PARTIAL SCANS
    An unreadable file is reported on stderr and recorded with a null
    ID; sockets, fifos, and devices are reported and omitted. The
    description (or snapshot) is still produced, and id exits 2.

FILES
    Store root: $C4_STORE, or the first store in ~/.c4/config, or
    ~/.c4/store. Journal: <store>/log.c4m — an ordinary c4m patch
    chain; one section per ingest. See c4-log(1).

EXIT STATUS
    0 success; 1 error; 2 partial scan (details on stderr)

EXAMPLES
    c4 id src/ > src.c4m            # describe (content form); no store
    c4 id -m f src/                 # full description with modes/times
    c4 id -q src/                   # content ID: same on every machine
    c4 id -s src/                   # snapshot; prints snapshot ID
    c4 id -q saved.c4m              # a saved description's own ID
    c4 id src/ | c4 id -q -         # pipe law: prints src's content ID
    c4 patch chain.c4m | c4 id -s - # store a resolved description

SEE ALSO
    c4 restore (materialize), c4 cat (read), c4 log (journal),
    c4 diff (compare), c4 gc (collect), c4 explain id
